sections.t: Deep East Texas, ring by ring
sections.x: East Texas Legacy Coalition. Count the rings. That’s us. Cut a longleaf pine in Angelina County and you can read its life in the rings: the wet years, the dry years, the fires it lived through. Deep East Texas reads the same way. Every ring below is a chapter, oldest at the heart. Tap one to jump to it. c. 800 Caddo build mounds on the Neches. 1690 First Spanish mission in Texas. 1779 Nacogdoches brought back to life. 1882 Rails reach a new town called Lufkin. 1894 Diboll’s sawmill fires up. 1936 Cutover land becomes national forest. 1940 The paper mill opens. 1974 Big Thicket protected. 2026 Us. A pine cross-section with one ring for each era of Deep East Texas history The center ring is about the year 800, when the Caddo built mounds near the Neches River. The outer ring is today. Each ring links to its part of the story below

sections.t: Deep East Texas, ring by ring
sections.h: Before Texas was Texas, it was Caddo country
sections.x: 800 Before Texas was Texas, it was Caddo country. Around the year 800, Caddo people chose a bluff above the Neches River, about 26 miles west of where Nacogdoches sits now, and built a permanent village and ceremonial center. Three earthen mounds still rise out of the pines there today, at Caddo Mounds State Historic Site near Alto. Here’s the part most folks don’t know: the name of this whole state came out of these woods. The Caddo word táyshaʼ meant “friend” or “ally.” The Spanish wrote it down as Tejas. That’s why the state motto is one word: Friendship. Sources: Texas Historical Commission, Caddo Mounds history (settled about A.D. 800); Texas Time Travel (THC) (26 miles west of Nacogdoches); Texas Beyond History, “Caddo Homeland” (taysha, friend or ally); TSHA Handbook of Texas , “Texas, Origin of Name” and the state motto entry. Watch: Koo-Hoo-Kiwat, the Caddo grass house A half-hour PBS program following a Caddo elder and his apprentice as they build a traditional grass house at Caddo Mounds. Visit Caddo Mounds 1649 State Hwy. 21 West, Alto. The Caddo Nation and the Texas Historical Commission now care for the site together. Sources: PBS program page ; Gilmer Mirror, Oct. 26, 2026 (joint stewardship)

sections.t: Deep East Texas, ring by ring
sections.x: 1690 The King’s Road comes through. Mission Tejas State Park, where a stretch of El Camino Real still runs through the pines. NPS photo, via National Park Service. In 1690 the Spanish built Mission San Francisco de los Tejas in a Caddo village near present-day Weches. It was the first mission in the province of Texas, and it didn’t last: by 1693 the friars had burned it and left. Smallpox struck in the winter of 1690 and killed almost 3,300 people in the area around the mission. The road they traveled, El Camino Real de los Tejas, is still out there. You can walk real wagon-worn stretches of it at Mission Tejas State Park and at Caddo Mounds. Texas Highway 21 follows much of the old route. Sources: Texas Parks and Wildlife, Mission Tejas history (1690, first mission in the province; Hwy 21); Texas Historical Commission marker 7013 ; National Park Service, Mission Tejas State Park (smallpox, almost 3,300 deaths, winter 1690; mission burned and abandoned Oct. 6, 1693). 1779: a town walks home. In 1773 Spain ordered its settlers out of East Texas. They didn’t stay gone. Antonio Gil Y’Barbo led them back, and in 1779 they rebuilt Nacogdoches on the old mission site. That’s why Nacogdoches calls itself the oldest town in Texas. Sources: SNAC record, Antonio Gil Y’Barbo papers (SFA East Texas Research Center and UT Libraries); National Register nomination, Nacogdoches

sections.h: Rails, sawdust and a brand-new town
sections.x: 1882 Rails, sawdust and a brand-new town. Lufkin didn’t exist until the Houston, East and West Texas Railway laid track through here in 1882. Lots went up for sale on Sept. 12 that year. The town was named for Abraham P. Lufkin, a Galveston cotton merchant. Then came the timber boom. In 1894 Temple built a sawmill on the same rail line and founded Diboll as a company town. Some mills moved whole communities from forest to forest as they cut. By the 1930s, a lot of the Piney Woods had been cut to the stump. sections.h: Cutover land gets a second chance
sections.x: 1936 Cutover land gets a second chance. In 1933 the Texas Legislature let the federal government buy up cutover timberland and worn-out farms. In 1936 President Franklin Roosevelt made four of them national forests: the Angelina, the Davy Crockett, the Sabine and the Sam Houston. The pines you drive through on the way to Sam Rayburn grew back on land that was once stumps. sections.x: 1940 The mill, and the water under it. Southland Paper Mills opened east of Lufkin in 1940 and became the biggest water user in Angelina County. sections.h: East Texans saved the Big Thicket
sections.x: 1974 East Texans saved the Big Thicket. Cypress knees in the Big Thicket. NPS photo by Scott Sharaga, via National Park Service. On Oct. 11, 1974, President Gerald Ford signed the law creating Big Thicket National Preserve, one of the first two national preserves in the country. It didn’t happen because Washington noticed. It happened because local people, starting with a meeting at the Saratoga Methodist Church in 1964, spent ten years refusing to quit. UNESCO now calls the Big Thicket a biosphere reserve. Carnivorous plants, cypress sloughs and American beech at the edge of its range, all a couple of hours down the road. Sources: National Park Service, 50th anniversary (Public Law 93-439, Oct. 11, 1974); NPS, “What is the Big Thicket?” ; Big Thicket Reporter #121 (1964 Saratoga meeting); Wikipedia (UNESCO biosphere reserve). People have called this place home for a long time. The Alabama and Coushatta tribes settled in the Big Thicket in the 1780s, and the Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas’s reservation sits right next to the preserve today. Homesteaders who did settle the thicket raised hogs and hunted with dogs. Source: NPS, “What is the Big Thicket?” Staley Cabin, a homestead log cabin in the Big Thicket. NPS photo by Scott Sharaga. Paddling a cypress slough on the Cooks Lake loop. NPS photo by Scott Sharaga. More Big Thicket videos The National Park Service’s full video library for the preserve. sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.x: The name. Angelina, the little angel. Long before there was a county, there was a young woman of the Hasinai, the Caddo people of these woods, whom the Spanish missionaries called Angelina, “little angel.” The river was named for her, and in 1846 the new county was named for the river. In 1976, for the nation’s bicentennial, the Angelina County Historical Survey Committee spent two years gathering records, family papers and hundreds of interviews into one book: Land of the Little Angel , edited by Lufkin newspaperman Bob Bowman. It’s still one of the fullest histories of the county. What follows are the stories from it we think everybody here ought to know. Angelina County at a glance. 1846 Created from Nacogdoches County. 1861 Voted against secession, 184 to 139. 1882 Railroad founds Lufkin at Denman Springs. 1892 Lufkin becomes the county seat. 1936 Angelina National Forest proclaimed. 1940 First newsprint from Southern pine. 1965 Sam Rayburn Reservoir dedicated. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976); Joe T. Timmons, “The Referendum in Texas on the Ordinance of Secession,” East Texas Historical Journal 11, no. 2. The Angelina River in fall, 2012. The History Center calls it the home of the Hainai. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.h: Salt springs, a mission and a land deed
sections.x: Before 1846. Salt springs, a mission and a land deed. The land was Hasinai and Bedias country long before it was a county. The county history repeats a legend of a mission founded at Angelina’s own village in July 1717, near the Linwood crossing of the Angelina River, and moved to San Antonio a decade later. In 1797 Bedias land was traded for goods to the Spanish-era trader Vicente Micheli, an early link in the county’s chain of land titles. Three salt springs. The county history and the 1937 Boon thesis describe three salines: two near Shawnee Creek and one on the Angelina. Salt water rising into shallow ground water was part of this landscape from the start. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 16; Effie Boon thesis (1937), p. 18. Water that gushed. An 1882 state report said springs and wells were numerous here. An 1882 visitor wrote that the county’s waters gushed forth in abundance and quality. Artesian wells, 390 to 1,200 feet deep, were in use by about 1920. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 22–23, 181; Ch. 2. The first census. In 1847 the state counted 834 people in the new county, 154 of them enslaved. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 9. Certificates that weren’t good. Before Texas independence, the Galveston Bay and Texas Land Company sold land certificates here that weren’t legal, the county’s first outside speculators. Most early settlers held Mexican grants dated 1834–35, under the empresarios Zavala and Vehlein. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 5. A grant still on the map. Stephen J. Stanley’s 4,432-acre Mexican land grant, from De Zavala’s colony, still shows on the county’s land maps. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 303. 1687 La Salle, as legend. The French explorer La Salle was killed by his own men in March 1687 somewhere in East Texas. The county history notes that some people believe he’s buried in Nacogdoches or Angelina County. Nobody knows the spot; a 1930 marker places it near Navasota. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 17–18; Texas State Library and Archives ; Navasota marker. The Fort Terán crossing on the Neches River. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.h: A courthouse on the move: four county seats
sections.x: 1846–1892. A courthouse on the move: four county seats. The county’s first election, in July 1846, drew only 139 votes. Its first Commissioners Court met at A. C. Caldwell’s home on Shawnee Prairie with a Mexican blanket thrown over a log for a desk. Then the fight over where the courthouse belonged lasted nearly half a century. 1857 No quorum, no deal. When commissioners tried to move the seat from Jonesville to Homer, Chief Justice Joseph Herrington objected that the law hadn’t been followed: a man who wasn’t a sworn commissioner had acted, and only three commissioners had done business when four were required. He declared their acts void. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 23. 1858 The recount. Some election returns were destroyed. The first certification gave Jonesville 124 votes to Homer’s 3. A recount from the election judges’ own records two days later gave Homer 221 and Jonesville 130. Homer won. The county clerk reportedly carried the records there on his shoulders. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 23–24, 145. 1891 The courthouse fire. Lufkin tried to take the county seat in 1885 and lost, 532 to 247. Then Homer’s courthouse burned. Homer folks blamed Lufkin night riders; nothing was ever proven. The county records survived in two safes, and Homer men guarded them for three days. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 24–26. 1892 Lufkin wins. On Jan. 2, 1892, Lufkin won the county seat, 1,076 to 436. Homer claimed Lufkin had brought in railroad hands, traveling salesmen and out-of-towners to vote. Lufkin had argued the land records belonged near the railroad, where land agents could get at them. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 26, 153. 1847 Court in the wrong house. On Feb. 1, 1847, lawyer T. J. Jennings of Nacogdoches objected that court was meeting at Isaac Dunagan’s home when the voters had made Marion the seat of justice. Judge Amos Clark agreed and moved all business to Marion. The first lawyer on record in the county won by pointing out that the process was wrong. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 215. Lufkin was born at a spring. The railroad reached a crossroads called Denman Springs in 1882, and when Lufkin incorporated in 1890 its city limits were drawn from “the head of Brushy Creek” and Denman Spring. In 1891 the town built its first waterworks, with a standpipe in the middle of Cotton Square. See Our water has a paper trail and Who decides the route. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 25, 152–153

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.x: 1861. The county that said no. On Feb. 23, 1861, Texans voted on whether to leave the Union. Statewide, secession won with about three of every four votes. Angelina County voted no, 184 to 139. Of the 35 counties historians count as East Texas, it was the only one where a majority voted against secession. In the 1859 governor’s race, the county history says, it had voted for Sam Houston, who opposed secession. Then, like nearly every county in the South, it sent its men. In September 1861 the county raised Company D of the 7th Texas Cavalry, part of Sibley’s Brigade. About 500 men from the county served. Dissent had a price. The county history tells of John D. Gann, the county’s first district clerk, who voted against secession but joined the army anyway. Home on furlough, he was dragged out by night riders and hanged; his body was found near Jack Creek, and his grave on his own land has never been found. His log house west of Lufkin, one of the oldest homes in the county, still stands, restored, with a state historical marker. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 28, 263, 268; Joe T. Timmons, “The Referendum in Texas on the Ordinance of Secession, February 23, 1861: The Vote,” East Texas Historical Journal 11, no. 2; county returns via VoteArchive ; East Texas Historical Journal (only East Texas county to reject secession)

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.h: When the county went to war
sections.x: Service. When the county went to war. 1917 Company M. In June 1917 Capt. Kit McConnico raised Company M of the 5th Texas Regiment: 159 men at first, 267 by September, from Lufkin, Huntington, Homer, Pollok, Diboll, Burke and more. The county history calls it the largest volunteer company raised in Texas. About 40 county men died in World War I. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 31–33. 1917 Four times the quota. About 50 women organized the county Red Cross on June 20, 1917. The county raised four times its quota in four days, and the women packed three meals for each of Company M’s men as they left for Camp Bowie. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 94–95. 1941–45 World War II. More than 140 county men died. Families planted victory gardens and women ran the businesses. The Huntington boys who didn’t come home are remembered by McMullen Memorial Library. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 33, 111–112. Korea and Vietnam. The county history counts six county dead in Korea and nearly 15 in Vietnam. Seventeen Spanish-American War veterans had their own camp by 1925. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 31, 33. Bill Wesley of Lufkin guarding Hideki Tojo, Japan’s wartime prime minister. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.h: Ferries, steamboats and a river that carried cotton
sections.x: 1840s–1900. Ferries, steamboats and a river that carried cotton. In 1844 Moses and Robert Patton proved the Angelina could carry freight, floating 192 bales of cotton down it on a barge. For the next few decades steamboats like the Laura worked their way up the Neches and the Angelina as far as Marion, hauling cotton to Sabine Pass. A ferry was a public trust. Every river crossing was licensed by the county. Ferrymen posted a $1,000 to $5,000 bond, paid a yearly tax and charged rates the court set: 10 cents for a man and horse, 5 cents on foot, 50 cents for a four-ox wagon. At high water, rates tripled. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 132. Stranded in 1877. In March 1877 the Laura sat stuck in low water for two weeks. They were too far upriver for the Gulf tides to help; only rain could float her. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 134. Why the boats stopped. After 1900, river travel died out. The county history lists the reasons: logs from the lumber boom, sandbars, and farmers plowing up the natural springs that fed the river. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 135. The county’s own history says it in plain words: when the springs were plowed up, the river lost water. Springs and groundwater keep our creeks and rivers running between rains. That’s why we watch every big well that wants to pump our aquifer. See We’ve watched our water drop before and Good water. The Houston East & West Texas Railway bridge over the Neches River, about 1910. That railroad reached Lufkin in 1882. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.x: One-room schools. School by the spring. The first schools were log cabins with split-log benches and a mud-and-stick fireplace, girls on one side and boys on the other. Lunch came in a syrup bucket: pork, sweet potatoes, a biscuit and syrup. Every school sent the children to the nearest spring for water, and they drank from a tin cup. Look at the old school and church names and you’ll see the water: Clear Springs, Sulphur Springs, Harmony Springs, Bayou Springs, Cordaway Springs, Baker Wells. Communities settled where the water was good. The Republic of Texas set aside four leagues of land, about 17,700 acres, in every county to pay for public schools; Angelina’s were surveyed in 1857. When the school term ran short, families paid tuition to keep the teacher for a last month, and teachers often worked that month for nothing. In 1902 the county had 88 school districts. By 1975 it had six. Grade school, San Augustine, April 1939. Russell Lee, Farm Security Administration. Library of Congress. Miss Rebecca’s handwriting. Lufkin teacher Rebecca Townsend created a handwriting course used in nearly 40 states. She kept a box of quarters for children without lunch money. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 54, 308. Huntington’s schools. Huntington’s first school opened in 1900 on the site of the Renfro home. A two-story brick school went up in 1914, the first 11th-grade class came in 1921, and from 1939 to 1959 the district was the Huntington Rural Schools, gathering in Oak Flat, Odell, Rocky Hill, Salem, Ora and more. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 56–57. Huntington’s story Bus number one. Concord School had some of the county’s first school buses, built by the Martin Wagon Co. in Lufkin. Concord is under Sam Rayburn Reservoir now. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 60. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 40–58

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.x: Religion in the pines. Brush arbors and a $13.60 bell. Many of the county’s churches started outdoors, under a brush arbor, after a revival. First Baptist Church of Huntington was organized that way in 1901, a week after a revival. Churches, like schools, went where the water was: Ryan Chapel near Burke was set on a hilltop by flowing springs, with water for the horses. Mrs. Abney’s Sunday school. Mrs. P. C. Abney couldn’t read or write. She taught herself so she could teach the Bible, and in 1878 she started the county’s first Sunday school with her own 12 children and the neighbors’ kids. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 65. The catalog bell. Ryan Chapel ordered its bell from Montgomery Ward in 1907 for $13.60. It rang for services, for emergencies and when a grave needed digging. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 65. Refused, then restored. In 1895 a visiting Episcopal priest couldn’t find a single house in Lufkin that would take him in and left after sitting under some scrub oaks. The church was built anyway. Decades later, the Lufkin Service League restored old St. Cyprian’s as a historical and arts center. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 81–82. A woman in the pulpit. The Rev. Emma Irick brought the Church of the Nazarene to Lufkin in 1910 and came back in the Depression to pastor it with no set salary. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 84. Worship at home. Lufkin’s Jewish families, here since about 1900, never built a temple. They held services in homes, like Harry Abram’s, and Dave Robinson spoke at local churches to build understanding. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 85. Church in the courthouse. For about eight years the Church of Christ held its services in the Angelina County courthouse. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 83

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.h: Sulphur Springs and the city that never was
sections.x: A mineral spring. Sulphur Springs and the city that never was. South of Zavalla, near today’s FM 1270, three springs of clear, strong-smelling sulphur water flowed by Sandy Creek. Families came by covered wagon and buggy to camp all summer and drink the water. In 1887 George and Henrietta Hawkins moved there hoping the water would cure her, and she recovered. Leading Lufkin families camped there for weeks at a time. Speculators saw a health resort. In 1892 the tract was surveyed into eight blocks of town lots for a “Sulphur City.” It never happened. Courthouse deeds show the tract was seized by the sheriff in March 1897 and sold at auction at the courthouse door. Later a lumber company camp and a turpentine camp brought people back for a while, and when the camps left, so did the town. Sulphur Springs is a reminder that our groundwater has a character of its own, and that people have always tried to sell it. The question then and now is who gets to profit from the water under our feet. See the Pineywoods rules and seven big projects. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 71–72, 275

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.x: 1880s–1930s. The timber kingdom. When the first settlers came, the pines stood more than 100 feet tall and four or five feet across. The county history says plainly that settlers saw the forest as an obstacle and gave no thought to conservation. Then the railroads came, and the big mills. 7,000 → 201,313 Acres, in 15 years. T. L. L. Temple bought about 7,000 acres from J. C. Diboll in the 1890s and started a mill. By 1908 his company held 201,313 acres. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 156–159. The company town. The mill companies built the houses, the church and the school, hired the teacher and ran the waterworks. Workers were paid in company tokens and scrip good only at the company store, which sold everything from cornmeal to caskets. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 115, 156–160, 184. He wouldn’t sell. At Pollok, Henry Claybon refused to sell his land to the mill. Instead he leased it, for 200 pounds of salt pork and four barrels of flour a year, for as long as the mill ran or 99 years. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 162. Turpentine. From 1923 to 1931 the McMillan Naval Stores Co. tapped about 23,000 acres of virgin longleaf in the county for turpentine. Black workers did nearly all of the work. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 185. Cut out and get out. Very few trees were replanted. When the timber ran out, the mills moved on and left hundreds of ghost towns behind. The cutover land was sold to the federal government for the national forests. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 185–188. How the forest came back The Hoo Hoo Band. Lufkin’s lumbermen had their own brotherhood, the Hoo Hoo, with a black cat for its emblem, and its own brass band. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 82, 91, 106, 230, 280. 1893 The World’s Fair pine. The 1893 Chicago World’s Fair used Southern pine for many of its buildings. The county history says that’s what opened the national market for it. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 182. The federal law behind our national forests, the 1911 Weeks Act, let the government buy land at the headwaters of navigable streams to protect the water. The Angelina National Forest was bought to protect a watershed. See Our water has a paper trail. Logging crews and mules on steep red clay hills near Fastrill, about 1930. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas. Diboll’s Timberland Theater in 1942. It opened in 1937 under a deal with the Southern Pine Lumber Company. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.h: Who owned the woods and the water
sections.x: Who held the land. Who owned the woods and the water. The county history doesn’t hide it: a small circle of families owned the mills, the railroads, the bank, the foundry and the paper. Here are the facts it records. The railroad’s secret route. Folks long told how the railroad skipped Homer because its surveyors got jailed after a rowdy night. SFA historian Robert Maxwell found in the railroad’s own papers that no right-of-way was ever sought at Homer; the route was set on paper years earlier, and the river crossing was bought in 1879. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 146–148. Knowing first. Col. Washington Lafayette Denman learned in the early 1880s where the railroad would run, bought a big tract northwest of Homer, and the line went right through the middle of it. The county history calls it the beginning of Lufkin and the end of Homer. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 216–217. Private woods. Private hunting and fishing clubs held huge tracts of river bottom: the Southern Pine Club, over 30,000 acres; the Pine Island Club, 5,400 acres with membership capped at 42; and the Malibou Club, built by Humble Oil in 1935 for its people. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 95–96. The office where it was decided. The county history says the building that held E. L. Kurth’s offices was where many of the key decisions of Angelina County were made. Kurth’s companies ran sawmills, a paper mill, railroads, banks, hotels, newspapers and radio. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 114, 169–170. Stumps for sale. In the Depression, Southern Pine Lumber sold the federal government 100,000 acres for under $3 an acre. Much of the national forest land had been, in the book’s words, severely cut before the sale. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 159, 187. 1917 One of the first city managers. Lufkin adopted the city-manager form in 1917, among the first towns in Texas to do it. The charter commission was chaired by Kester Denman, whose grandfather gave the railroad its right-of-way in 1882. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 153. Dreams from outside. Boston investors and the Manton orchard. A French lawyer’s tobacco plantation north of Lufkin, abandoned by 1917. A Chicago group’s plan to settle hundreds of Dutch farm families here, never carried out. A tung oil orchard south of Zavalla that failed. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 89–90, 192–193, 196, 222. 1940 Who sets the values. In 1940 Hudson schools went independent so they could raise property values above what the county set and fund their own schools. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 52. 1935 278,000 acres. When T. L. L. Temple died in 1935, his companies held about 278,000 acres of East Texas timberland. He had started in the 1890s with about 7,000 acres bought from J. C. Diboll. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 115–117, 305. Odum’s Town. The county history says Durant was nicknamed “Odum’s Town” for the power of Louie G. Odum, who was a county commissioner, the sawmill owner and the first postmaster, all at once. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 176. 1934 The paper and the mill. In 1914 J. H. Kurth Sr. of the Angelina County Lumber Co. became one of three owners of the Lufkin Daily News. In 1932 the paper printed a record 50-page edition promoting the proposed newsprint mill. In 1934 Kurth, W. C. Trout and the Henderson family bought the paper, and on Jan. 14, 1940, it ran a 288-page edition celebrating Southland Paper Mills. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 203–208. Keltys, born Klein. Charles Louis Kelty was born Klein in Alsace and took his mother’s maiden name. He came in 1859 and built the mill at Keltys with his son-in-law. J. H. Kurth Sr. later bought it, and it grew into the Angelina County Lumber Co. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 167, 279–280. From the chamber to the newsroom. W. R. Beaumier went from managing the Chamber of Commerce to running the Lufkin Daily News, from 1943 to 1965. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 203–208. 1973 A seat in the House. In 1973 Arthur Temple III of Diboll, of the Temple timber family, followed John Hannah into the Texas House. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 35. Graves inside a pump station. At Redland, the county history says, a pioneer family’s graves lie inside the Gulf pump station, and later members of that family worked for the pipeline. Whether the graves are still there, and who can visit them, is worth asking. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 170, 255. The pattern is old: whoever knows first where the railroad, the highway or the pipeline will go decides who prospers. That’s why we file records requests before the deals are done. See Who decides the route and our records requests

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.h: The water districts most people never heard of
sections.x: Water on the books. The water districts most people never heard of. The county history lists the public bodies with power over our water as of 1976. Some still exist. Some may be sitting dormant with powers nobody uses. 1935 A river authority. Created in 1935 as the Sabine-Neches Conservation District, cut back to the Neches and Angelina basins in 1949, dormant in the 1960s, revived in the 1970s, with a board appointed by the governor. Today it’s the Angelina & Neches River Authority. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 193. 1957 WCID No. 2. Commissioners created Angelina County Water Control and Improvement District No. 2 in 1957, covering about 640,000 acres, more than the whole county’s 514,368. Does it still exist, and what can it do? That’s a question for a records request. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 181, 193. Soil and water. Landowners formed the Upper Neches Soil Conservation District after World War II because topsoil was washing off their farms. Cotton fell from 8,000 acres in 1947 to 390 in 1963. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 193. A canal on paper. A Deep East Texas Inter-Basin Navigation District was created to study a canal between Sam Rayburn and Toledo Bend. It never got going. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 193. Wood treating. A creosote wood-treating plant went up in 1938 on the old Lufkin Land mill site in East Lufkin, another opened nearby in 1946, and Southern Pine opened one at Diboll in 1951. Every old sawmill also had its log pond. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 124, 185. Lignite. The county history noted lignite in the Yegua-Jackson layers and predicted power companies might want it someday. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 192. 1900 Rain-water soda. In 1900 the Lufkin Steam Bottling Works made its sodas, it said, from pure rain water. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 126. 1966 Fresh Water Supply District No. 1. The Commissioners Court created Angelina County Fresh Water Supply District No. 1 in 1966, covering about 1,498 acres. It sold $120,000 in bonds in 1970. Another district, formed with Nacogdoches County in 1954, runs Lake Striker. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 193. Old industrial ground and forgotten water districts are exactly what we look up when a new project shows up. See seven big projects and where you get a say

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.h: From sawmill repair shop to the oil fields of the world
sections.x: 1902–today. From sawmill repair shop to the oil fields of the world. Lufkin Foundry and Machine Co. opened in 1902 to fix sawmill machinery, which until then had to be shipped to St. Louis. W. C. Trout became its manager in 1905. After talks with Humble Oil, the foundry built its first enclosed-gear oil pumping unit in 1923. Trout sketched an adjustable counterbalance crank, the story goes, on a tablecloth; the patent was granted in 1926. By 1971 the company had shipped its 100,000th unit. Its engineers had patents of their own. One of them, Fred Graham, married a country schoolteacher from Oak Flat. Read his story. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 117–122, 309; Google Patents, US 2,048,119

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.x: Before Titusville? Oil at Tar Spring. Most histories give Lyne Barret of Nacogdoches County credit for the first oil well in Texas, in 1866. The county history makes a claim for one of our own. Citing a 1946 article in the Southwestern Historical Quarterly , it says that shortly before 1859 a man named Jack Graham dug a pit near “Tar Spring” in Angelina County and collected oil from it. Oil seeps were fairly common here when settlers arrived. They used the oil to grease wagon wheels and harness. The county’s first producing oil well came in near Ewing in 1923. Oil came to the surface here at springs, rising with the groundwater. Where water moves up, it can move down. That’s one reason we ask hard questions about anything that gets injected, stored or spilled over our aquifer. See where you get a say. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 191–192, citing C. A. Warner, Southwestern Historical Quarterly , July 1946

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.x: Gone but not forgotten. Ghost towns of Angelina County. The National Archives records more than 50 post offices in the county. Most of the towns behind them are gone. Some died when the timber ran out, some when the railroad passed them by, and some went under the lake. Marion The first county seat, 1846–1854, at Moses Bluff on the Angelina. Steamboats stopped there. Its post office ran from 1847 to 1876. Jonesville County seat 1854–1858, about three miles southeast of present Huntington. The county just rented a house; no courthouse was ever built. The cemetery remains. Homer County seat 1858–1892, named by Dr. W. W. Manning for Homer, Louisiana. It faded after the railroad passed six miles to the northwest. Cheeseland North of Pollok, settled in the 1840s and known for the cheese its Dutch-French families made. Jacob Humphrey’s 1844 stockade still stood in 1976. Acol The Angelina County Lumber Co.’s post office was a boxcar on rails. When the logging camp moved, the post office rolled along with it. Manton Boston investors bought about 12,500 acres of logged-over land east of Lufkin and planted 1,000 acres of peaches, pears and plums in 1902. The orchard failed; by 1914 the dream was gone. Micheli A sawmill town of about 1,000 on the old Micheli Spanish land grant, one of the few mills to float its logs down the Angelina. Bankrupt by 1906. Ora Between Huntington and the Angelina River. Its postmaster named it for his baby daughter, Ora Medford, in 1884. She grew up to run Kurth Memorial Library for 29 years. Concord Founded around a little plank church in 1860, gone exactly a hundred years later under Sam Rayburn Reservoir. Seven cemeteries were moved. Bug Tussle A one-room log school near Renfro Prairie, on the Emporia logging front. In summer the ticks and gnats swarmed the children. Bodan Near Pollok, named for a Frenchman’s store on the old Smuggler’s Trail. Bodan Cemetery straddles the old road. Yuno, Krub, Jake, Retrieve Just a few of the more than 50 post offices the National Archives lists for the county. Most are only names now. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 21–31, 45–46, 143–180, 221–222, 293. What’s left of the Aldridge Lumber Company mill at Aldridge, a sawmill town that died when the timber ran out. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.h: Festivals, clubs and the corner store
sections.x: Town life. Festivals, clubs and the corner store. 1938 The Texas Forest Festival. Begun in 1938 on the ground where Lufkin High stands now: lumbering contests, forestry exhibits, a two-mile parade and as many as 40,000 visitors. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 90–91. Opera house to picture show. The Lufkin Opera House opened in 1909 and burned in 1920. Movies came in 1913. In 1948 the Dallas Symphony played to 1,200 people. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 91–93. The women’s clubs. The Historical and Literary Club (1909) started Lufkin’s first kindergarten in 1920. The Athenian Forum (1933) debated Darwin, Mussolini and capital punishment. By 1941 there were 21 clubs. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 97–101. 1933 A library from a bequest. Kurth Memorial Library was built in 1933 from J. H. Kurth Sr.’s $10,000 gift for the town’s greatest civic need. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 110. A bird sanctuary. The Lufkin Garden Club worked five years to make Lufkin a bird sanctuary and won state and national awards for it. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 102. Milk for schoolchildren. From 1936 until after World War II the Rotary Anns gave about 10,000 pints of milk a year to underfed children, and teachers reported better grades. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 100. Born on the square. Brookshire Brothers opened on the courthouse square in 1921. Perry Brothers grew from a nickel store into a big regional chain. Atkinson Candy began in 1932. Kerr’s, founded at Homer in 1870, was the county’s oldest business. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 113, 127–130, 257, 297. A flying saucer attack. To sell Buddy Poppies, veterans staged a flying saucer attack on Lufkin, dropping paper saucers from a plane. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 94. Six-man football. The county history credits Diboll with the first six-man football team in Texas, and Diboll’s T. L. L. Temple Memorial Library was the 1968 Texas Library of the Year. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 159–161. 1905 Country doctors. Folks waited until someone was very sick to send for the doctor, who came by horse and buggy. Doctors collected only about three-fourths of their fees, often in eggs, butter and produce. Lufkin’s first hospital opened in 1905–06 under Dr. A. M. Denman, with the county’s first X-ray machine, and the county hospital opened in 1919. Old remedies belong in history books, not medicine cabinets. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 211–213. 1949 A hospital the mills built. Memorial Hospital opened in 1949 as a private hospital started by E. L. Kurth Sr., W. C. Trout and Col. C. C. Chambers, and backed by local industry. Gov. Beauford Jester came for the dedication on May 12, 1949. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 212. 1915 For a dry town. A 1915 photo in the county history shows a temperance rally in downtown Lufkin, with signs asking voters to make it a dry town. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 177. The Diboll Millers. The county’s last semi-pro baseball team played into the mid-1950s at Miller Stadium, which Southern Pine Lumber Co. built across U.S. 59. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 238. Lufkin’s Southern Pacific passenger depot, about 1959. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.x: Angelina County’s who’s who. People worth knowing. Zavalla Cmdr. Arthur Ray Hawkins. Born in Zavalla in 1922, he became one of the Navy’s top aces of World War II, with 14 aerial victories and three Navy Crosses, and later led the Blue Angels. Lufkin aviator A. O. McQueen taught him to fly. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 141–142; National Aviation Hall of Fame. Angelina County W. D. Gann. Born in the county in 1878, he went from selling newspapers on the train to trading on Wall Street and wrote books on market forecasting that traders still argue about today. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 270; Wikipedia. Lufkin Gov. Allan Shivers. Born in Lufkin on Oct. 5, 1907, he became governor of Texas and chaired the Interstate Oil Compact Commission. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 37–38, 317. Homer Beulah Watts. Born at Homer in 1873, she took up painting at 40 and left about 1,000 paintings of East Texas pines, shown across the country. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 310. Lufkin Miss Gussie Wilson. In 1900 she bought the Lufkin Leader. The county history calls her Lufkin’s only known woman editor. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 205. Huntington Charlie B. Adams. A woman coached Huntington’s boys to county titles on outdoor courts from about 1918 to 1922. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 244. Lufkin “Aunt Liza”. Maudice Smith, who played Aunt Liza on KTRE radio, won the Texas Story Telling Festival in 1944 and tied for second in the nation in 1946. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 101. Angelina County Rep. John Hannah. One of the reform-minded “Dirty Thirty” legislators in the Sharpstown scandal years, later district attorney, then a lobbyist for Common Cause Texas. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 35–37, 217. Texas Forest Service The smoke chaser. Knox Ivie was hired in 1928 at $85 a month to watch for fires from a crow’s nest in a tall hickory. A tree cab he built was struck by lightning hours after he finished it, and at night he heard wolves. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 189–190. Ottis E. Lock. Ten years in the Texas House and ten in the Senate, the county’s longest legislative tenure, and an author of the Gilmer-Aikin school laws. He retired as a Southland Paper vice president. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 35–36, 284. Ora Medford McMullen. The baby the town of Ora was named for. She ran Kurth Memorial Library from 1932 to 1961, and its genealogy room bears her name. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 86, 293. Jesse Kellam. Lufkin’s football coach from 1923 to 1930, who named the team the Panthers, later became a close associate of Lyndon Johnson in broadcasting. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 240. Homer Garrison Jr. The Lufkin native who led the Texas Department of Public Safety for decades. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 38. Dr. J. E. Peavy Jr. Lufkin’s own Texas commissioner of health. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 38, 295. Annie Lee Jones. Coached Huntington’s first girls’ basketball team, in 1929–30. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 245. J. J. Collins. Born on an Angelina County farm in 1891, he taught in one- and two-room schools and finished law school in a year. He defended more than 100 murder cases, lost fewer than 12, and never had a client sentenced to death. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 215–218. W. J. Townsend Sr. A Homer lawyer, he wrote the state law making hog theft a felony, organized a bank, helped start the Lufkin school district, served as county judge, and with Eugene Blount developed Huntington. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 307. Also from the county: Pete Runnels, two-time American League batting champion, and sportswriter Morris Frank (pp. 231–237). Dunbar High School’s champions are on our Black heritage page

sections.t: Land of the Little Angel: Angelina County history
sections.x: Gospel or gossip. Tall tales and true stories. The county history admits that some of its favorite stories mix fact, fiction and fancy, and nobody can tell which is which anymore. Enjoy them that way. 1913 The dynamited depot. On a Sunday night in March 1913 the Lufkin depot was blown up. The only man on duty vanished, and bones in the rubble let his family collect insurance. A detective later traced him by his handwriting to California. He was tried and acquitted. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 219–220. The corn rebellion. During Reconstruction, the women of Homer held down a federal corn agent and hauled the stored corn home. Nobody was ever punished. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 224. Ottie the mare. She pulled Lufkin’s first ice cream wagon in 1896 and answered the fire alarm on her own. She has a marker near Glendale Cemetery. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 225–226. Hobo. A three-legged dog in 1940s Lufkin, fed by the whole town and patched up by the foundry workers. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 229. 1938 Wrong Way Corrigan. The famous “wrong way” flier landed in Lufkin in 1938, and about 5,000 people turned out to see him. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 221. The dog ate the evidence. In an early hog-theft trial at Marion, a dog ate the evidence, the hog’s ears, during the lunch recess, and the case was dismissed. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 37. The champion farkleberry. In 1976 the national champion farkleberry tree stood near Zavalla, 29 feet tall, in the creek country of Sandy, Turpentine, Shawnee and Possum Walk creeks. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 221. Get along, little doggies. Turned down for a loan in the Depression, rancher Doc Roach drove his whole herd up to the banker’s window. He got the money. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 223–224. 1856 The Moore farm mystery. In August 1856 Abram Moore, his wife Peggy and a child were shot at supper on their Angelina River plantation. Nobody was caught. Legend says he buried gold under a tree guarded by a chained bear. The court fight that followed turned on which of them died last. The land is under Sam Rayburn now. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 229–230. Hogs in the jail. W. M. Glenn won the mayor’s race in 1899 promising to pen the loose hogs, and ended up keeping them in the city jail. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 222, 272. The Antlers Hotel. Southern Pine’s log inn at Diboll did fine until U.S. 59 was rerouted around it. It closed and was burned in 1953 because it couldn’t be torn down. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 223. A knight from Lufkin. Leland Thomas Jordan, 32 years with Gulf Oil and 14 in Kuwait, received an honorary British knighthood in 1961. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 226–227. Unlucky thirteens. The Hoo Hoo Band’s 1902 trip to Milwaukee ran into a string of 13s, including two train wrecks. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 230. 1956 The tree that beat the clock. The new courthouse got a $1,387 clock, and an oak tree hid it. The Lufkin Daily News printed ballots, and the tree won, 693 to 194. It was an election year, and the commissioners honored the vote. Ten years later, at a beautification committee’s urging, officials quietly had the tree trimmed, and nobody protested. By then the clock hadn’t run in a decade. A win that isn’t written down can be undone without a vote. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 228

Angelina County Black heritage in the pines. Black families built this county: its mills, its farms, its churches and schools, and some of the finest athletes Texas ever produced. Here are their stories, told plainly, from the records and from the community’s own memory

sections.h: The people whose work built the first mills
sections.x: Before 1865. The people whose work built the first mills. Slavery was part of Angelina County from the start. The 1847 state census counted 154 enslaved people among the county’s 834 residents. By 1850 the number was 196, and by 1860 it was 686. On James Ewing’s plantation on the Angelina River, a few miles northeast of Ora near present-day Huntington, enslaved people ran a gristmill, a cotton gin, a cane mill, a blacksmith shop and a brick kiln, and drove cattle and hogs all the way to Natchitoches, Louisiana. At the county’s water-powered mill on Mill Creek, built in 1853, the county history names one of the men who worked it: Berry Roberts, who was enslaved. In 1936 he was said to be still living near the old mill site, over 90 years old. The records that treated people as property are also, now, a way to find them. When Abram and Peggy Moore were killed in 1856, the probate inventory of their estate listed 33 enslaved people. Records like these can help descendants trace their families, and the county’s probate files survive with the Angelina County Clerk. Enslaved people in the county. 1847 154 of 834 residents. 1850 196. 1860 686. For descendants. 1850 and 1860 federal slave schedules. Angelina County probate records (Moore estate, 1856–1861). Our family research guide. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 9, 182, 197–198, 229–230. The county’s first industry ran on water power and enslaved labor. Read the Mill Creek story and Our water has a paper trail

Freedom came late to Texas. George Hackney. George Hackney was born into slavery in Tennessee in 1833. As a young man he and his brothers and sisters were sold at the New Orleans slave market, and James Ewing bought him and brought him to the Angelina River. He worked the Ewing plantation as a blacksmith and a teamster, hauling cotton by ox team to Alto. The news of freedom reached them on June 19, 1865, the day Texans now celebrate as Juneteenth. According to the county history, Ewing told Hackney he could go, and threatened to kill him if he stopped within a hundred miles. He left with what he owned in a flour sack. He settled in Lufkin anyway, bought land and town lots, ran a boarding house, and met the night trains to see travelers safely to their beds. The county history notes he was one of the few Black men who could be seen in town after dark. His son Joe bought 50 acres at Homer. His grandson Hugh went to Texas College. He was told to go and keep going. He stayed, bought land, and spent his nights making sure strangers got home safe. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 51, 199–200, 274–275

Land that stayed in the family. Squire “Uncle Square” Long. After the war, Squire Long, a freedman known to everyone as Uncle Square, bought a homestead next to a white neighbor’s farm. In 1974 his descendants still owned it. He was a Freemason and built and kept up chapels that served Black families as both church and school. In 1892 Long Chapel C.M.E. Church was organized on the old Square Long property. Its founders were Square Long, Will Roberts, Jacob Roberts, John Burton and Mahalia Long. Members put up a church building in 1908, and the present one in 1948. It’s an early Black congregation, still part of the county’s story. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 71, 291–292

sections.h: Churches that held the community together
sections.x: Faith. Churches that held the community together. 1892 Long Chapel C.M.E. Organized by Father Mims on the Square Long property. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 71. 1902 Goodwill Baptist. Began under a brush arbor in the Lufkin Land mill community. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 75

sections.h: Schools built by and for the community
sections.x: Education. Schools built by and for the community. Lufkin’s first Black school stood on Chestnut Street near Paul Avenue and later moved to Leach Street. Keltys had its own school west of the railroad tracks. Over the years came Carver, Brandon and Dunbar, the heart of Black Lufkin for decades. 1923 Dunbar School. Built on Lake Street. W. H. Brandon was its principal in 1939. Brandon School followed in 1946. Dunbar was merged into Lufkin High at integration. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 49, 200, 202, 245. 1964 Hackney Elementary. Carver School, built in 1939–40, was renamed for Olivia Ray Hackney, who had taught at Dunbar since 1931. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 50–51, 200. 1948 Mabel Melear School. The Keltys school was renamed for its principal, Mabel Melear. The old Leach Street school became Melinda Garrett Elementary. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 49. 1960s Integration. Diboll integrated its schools by 1968, ahead of most of the region. Lufkin completed integration of every campus between 1969 and 1974. In Huntington, a separate school for Black students was still being built in 1961. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 51, 55, 57, 161. H.G. Temple School, Diboll’s school for Black students, in 1953 and in 2009. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas. An early H.G. Temple senior class, about 1944 or 1945. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas. The H.G. Temple High School band, 1955. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas

1953–1969. The Dunbar era. For about 16 years, Lufkin’s Dunbar High School was one of the great athletic programs in Texas. Under coach Elmer Redd the Dunbar Tigers won three state football championships, going 143–35. Dunbar also won three state track titles and six state tennis titles. Curtis Mills, a Lufkin native, set the world record in the 440-yard dash, 44.7 seconds, at Texas A&M in 1969. Dunbar’s Phillip Jones played national tennis, including against Arthur Ashe. Ken Houston went from Dunbar to the Houston Oilers and Washington and into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. When Dunbar was merged into Lufkin High, the county history gave the whole era one paragraph. It deserves a lot more than that, and we’d like to help tell it. Outstanding citizens the county history names (partial). Elmer Redd , coach; three state football titles, later an assistant at the University of Houston. Curtis Mills , world record, 440 yards. Ken Houston , Pro Football Hall of Fame. Joe H. Williams , Dallas Cowboys, 1972 Super Bowl. Clifford Brooks , Baltimore Colts. D. C. Nobles , quarterback, University of Houston. Willie Spencer , first Black official in the Southwest Conference. Phillip Jones , national tennis. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 200–202, 245; Pro Football Hall of Fame

sections.h: Business, clubs and a Chamber of Commerce of their own
sections.x: Building up. Business, clubs and a Chamber of Commerce of their own. In 1955 a Dunbar civics class surveyed Black-owned businesses in Lufkin and counted 4 barber shops, 17 beauty shops, 2 mortuaries, 10 cafés, 5 construction firms, 8 groceries, 3 garages, 3 hotels, 2 taxi companies, 3 service stations, a newsstand, a blacksmith and 2 washaterias. 1940 Lufkin Citizens Chamber of Commerce. Founded by Dunbar principal F. W. Thomas. It bought band instruments for Dunbar, improved Jones Lake Park, opened a day care center for working mothers (the idea of E. E. Cleaver) and pushed for new housing near old Dunbar. It published a paper, The Mirror. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 199–200, 320–322. Garden and study clubs. The Progressive Garden Club (1936, Mrs. Hugh Hackney), the Community Aid Club (1941, Walter Ford of Keltys; 147 members by 1976), the Delphian Civic, Social and Study Club (1956; college scholarships) and the C. Mark Social and Charity Club (1967). Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 199–200. Firsts. In 1969 Olivia and Hugh Hackney became the first Black couple named the Lufkin Booster Club’s “Boosters of the Month.”. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 200

A remarkable life. “The Professor” of Diboll. William James Jackson died in Diboll on Nov. 19, 1972, just short of his 103rd birthday. According to the county history he was born in Milwaukee in the 1870s, grew up traveling with a medicine show, and spent 60 years in minstrel and circus bands. The book says he taught a young Harry James to play the trumpet and toured with W. C. Handy, playing in the band that introduced the “Memphis Blues” and the “St. Louis Blues.” He came to Diboll in the 1920s and worked 20 years as a porter and mail clerk on the Texas South-Eastern Railroad. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 198–199

Help us tell it right. Most of this page comes from Land of the Little Angel , a 1976 county history written mostly by descendants of white settlers. It holds names and dates we couldn’t find anywhere else, but it tells these stories from the outside, and some of its language is out of date. We’ve retold them in our own words.
