sections.x: A Piney Woods family · Oak Flat, near Huntington Under the black gum tree. In 2013 Winnie Graham wrote down 165 years of one family’s life in these woods: the Renfros, Browns, Sowells, Russells and Grahams of Oak Flat. It’s our founder’s family, and it’s the Piney Woods story of a lot of families. Here it is, retold in our own words. Staley Cabin, a homestead log cabin in the Big Thicket (not Oak Flat). NPS photo by Scott Sharaga

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.h: A family’s tales, and the woods kept butting in
sections.x: The book. A family’s tales, and the woods kept butting in. Winnie Graham grew up in Lufkin and spent her summers at her grandparents’ place at Oak Flat, several miles outside Huntington. She earned an engineering degree, and years later she sat down to write a few family stories for the younger generation. What came out was Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods , published by Stephen F. Austin State University Press in 2013. It’s a family memoir, but it’s also a field guide to how people lived here: what they ate, how they talked, what they sang, how they built and plowed and doctored their stock. Winnie was our founder’s kin. Everything on this page comes from her book unless we say otherwise. Where her history slipped (she was writing from memory and family lore, and a few dates are off), we checked it against the record and tell you what the record says. The family in this story. John Folkner Renfro and Rebecca Harrison Hicks , Renfro Prairie, 1840. Margaret Lucinda Renfro , “Granny Hutch,” 1838–1925. Catherine “Kate” Brown , “Grandma Wade,” 1863–1953. W. D. “Bill” Russell , 1848–1942, and Mary Chestnut Russell , 1852–1913. William Eli Russell , 1875–1952, and Leah Sowell Russell , 1884–1976. Lillian Russell Graham , 1903–1961, and Fred Graham , d. 1953. Winnie Graham , the author, born 1933. Sources: family chart in Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 12–13

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.h: Oak Flat, and the tree that named the book
sections.x: The place. Oak Flat, and the tree that named the book. Oak Flat is a farm settlement in the woods several miles outside Huntington, about 15 miles south of Lufkin. Winnie’s grandfather, Eli Russell, farmed a field there, and in that field stood a black gum tree. Generations later Winnie and her brothers still owned parcels of Grandpa’s field, and they planted it back in pines. The settlement had a one-room church house lit by coal oil lamps, and before World War I folks held brush arbor revivals there. The county’s own records count 19 pupils at the Oak Flat school in 1895, meeting in the church. Winnie remembered a two-room schoolhouse; when the country schools consolidated, she wrote, it was moved to the Huntington campus. Oak Flat School No. 47 joined the Huntington rural high school district in 1939. Later there were two painted churches, Baptist and Pentecostal. The Pentecostal one was Grandma Leah’s doing. Grandpa deeded just under an acre out of his cornfield, neighbors and kin built a plain one-room box church with no plumbing or lights, and young Winnie painted the sign with brushes she made out of rags. Services ran about five years. The building was later hauled off, and the acre has gone back to thicket. Today the field is pines again. You can still find old house places in these woods by the jonquils and the scraggly roses somebody planted by a door. Winnie’s tip for spotting a vanished homestead, from Under the Blackgum Tree. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 16–17, 49–57, 164–177; Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 42 (Oak Flat school, 1895); Oak Flat School No. 47 consolidation (1939) from The History Center, Diboll

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.x: How they got here. From Tennessee, Missouri and Arkansas. Winnie traced the family into Texas in three waves: one branch from Tennessee in 1838, one from Missouri in 1839, and one from Arkansas in 1853. Some settled first in Nacogdoches and San Augustine counties before landing in what’s now Angelina County. One story came down about a little girl on the trip in, around 1839, crossing a river so wide and rough that when she got thirsty she drank from her own shoe. Nobody remembers which river. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 15, 21

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.x: The schoolmakers. The Renfros of Renfro Prairie. John Folkner Renfro was born in Kentucky in 1797. He married Rebecca Harrison Hicks in Missouri, and in 1839 they brought their family to Texas: a year in Sabine County, then, in 1840, a homestead on what came to be called Renfro Prairie in Angelina County. The county history says one of the first known schools in the county stood near his home, and in 1848 the Renfro place served as a polling place. The prairie’s community is called Beulah today. What’s left of the home place, according to the county history: the first Renfro Cemetery, where he’s buried, an old cistern, and the cedar and crepe myrtle trees that marked the yard. 1840 A school on the prairie. One of Angelina County’s first known schools stood near the Renfro home. In 1895 the Renfro Prairie school had 24 pupils. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 41–42, 299. 1900 Huntington’s first school. John F. Renfro, the pioneer’s grandson, graduated from Sam Houston Normal in 1899. Huntington’s first school opened in 1900 on the site of the Renfro home, and from 1903 to 1913 the school ran on John Renfro’s property. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 56, 299. 1927 Huntington’s man in Austin. The same John F. Renfro, a Huntington landowner, banker and ordained minister, served in the Texas House from 1927 to 1931. The county history calls him an organizer and the second president of Huntington Guaranty State Bank. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 35, 299; Texas Legislative Reference Library, Texas Legislators: Past and Present

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.x: Two women who held it together. Granny Hutch and Grandma Wade. John Renfro’s daughter, Margaret Lucinda, was born in Missouri in 1838 and came to Texas as a baby. She married John E. Brown on July 4, 1858. He went off to the Civil War in 1862, wrote letters home, and was never heard from again. Their daughter Kate was born in April 1863 and never knew him. Margaret married again, to Aaron Hutchinson, an English-born Confederate cavalryman, and the family called her Granny Hutch from then on. After he died she drew a Confederate widow’s pension on his service. She lived until 1925. Her daughter Kate grew up to be Grandma Wade, and she lived to be 90. She married Pat Sowell at 17 and settled around Smyrna, a cotton community the family called “Smernie.” Pat died in 1889, when their daughter Leah was five, and Kate raised her children through hard years. She outlived more than one husband and kept her independence: in her late 70s she bought a little house in Huntington, had it moved out to Oak Flat and made it a wallpapered cottage. She did the family’s churning until the end. Grandma Wade’s ink. When she was young, folks made their own ink from oak galls. She’d forgotten the recipe, so when the children tried it they got only invisible ink. The missing piece was iron. Winnie’s version: crush a gall, stir it into water, drop in a rusty nail and let it sit for weeks. Sources: Winnie Graham, Listening to Plants: A Pathway to New Uses (2020), pp. 9–11. Grandma Wade’s owl. She’d call to the barred owls the old way, “who cooks for you all,” and Winnie said sometimes an owl would answer. Birders still teach that same phrase to learn the barred owl’s call. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 65–66. Grandma Wade’s rhymes. She had a verse for everything, from “Incie, pincie, cootsie corn” to “Up a hickory, down a pine.” Winnie wrote down a handful so they wouldn’t be lost. Find them in the book. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 65–66

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.x: The county’s last Confederate veteran. Grandpa Bill Russell. W. D. “Bill” Russell was born in Dallas County, Arkansas, in 1848 and came to Texas as a little boy of five. Near the very end of the Civil War, still a teenager, he joined up and was sent to Galveston. When it was over he walked home with the other boys, and Winnie wrote that a farm wife along the way fed them milk and cornbread. He married Mary Chestnut, and they raised ten children. When he died in 1942 the county history counted him as Angelina County’s last surviving Confederate veteran. He’s buried at Jonesville Cemetery near Huntington. In 1934 a University of Texas student writing the first scholarly history of the county interviewed a W. D. Russell of Huntington about the old days. Mary sent her son Eli a rose for his birthday. He rooted it and planted it in the middle of the cornfield, and for years the plowing went around it. From Under the Blackgum Tree. Bill walked with a hickory cane that had been carved by hand by a formerly enslaved man in Alabama, cut with the words “Jesus, Walk With Me Today.” It broke once and was wrapped with wire, and it stayed in the family. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 28–35; Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 300; Effie Boon, The History of Angelina County (master’s thesis, University of Texas, 1937), list of interviews

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.h: Eli and Leah Russell of Oak Flat
sections.x: Grandpa and Grandma. Eli and Leah Russell of Oak Flat. William Eli Russell got about eight grades in a one-room school and learned the rest from the land: plowing, beekeeping, doctoring livestock. Winnie said he could walk straight to the wild plums, magnolias and persimmons in the woods with no trail. As a young man he drove a log wagon for a timber company and “batched” in a cabin in the woods. He won the ring at a Riding the Ring contest, a horseback tournament where riders speared hanging rings at a gallop, and then gave his prize to a different girl, which made Leah jealous. They married anyway, on March 9, 1901. He became the settlement’s stand-in veterinarian. He built a banjo as a boy out of a hardwood disk and a cowhide head, later played the fiddle, and kept a blacksmith setup under an oak. He made chair bottoms out of hardwood inner bark and was known for them. He built twelve-room purple martin houses on tall poles and grew watermelons on contour rows the county agents helped farmers lay out to hold the soil and water. When he died in 1952, Winnie wrote, every store in town but one closed for his funeral. Leah Azeta Sowell was born in Smyrna in 1884 and rode double with her brother on his horse to the Old Smyrna school. She picked cotton, made quilts and sunbonnets, wheelbarrowed in topsoil for her hollyhocks, zinnias, okra and tomatoes, and loved three things best: ice cream, church and fishing. She fished with a cane pole, standing up, never sitting, and kept her own earthworm bed fed on coffee grounds. Dale Blanton Russell (1919–2014), Eli and Leah’s youngest, in his later years. Family photo. Their children. Lillian , 1903. Winnie , 1906, the aunt the author was named for. Mary Katherine , 1914. Dale , 1919. Read more. Riding the Ring. Dog-trots, gal’ries and party lines. What they ate. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 60–83, 138–177, 189–191

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.x: A Piney Woods girl goes to college. Lillian Russell, ballplayer and schoolteacher. Lillian went barefoot to school and hid her shoes behind a log. When the 1918 flu came through Oak Flat she was 15, and she nursed sick neighbors day and night. She played on the Huntington girls’ basketball team in bloomers, finished high school in 1920 at 17, and in 1921 went off to Sam Houston Normal in Huntsville, where she picked up the nickname “Diddie.”. From 20 on she taught in one- and two-room country schools at Oak Flat, Ora and Etoile, across the Angelina River from Huntington, and took summer courses at Stephen F. Austin in Nacogdoches and Southwest Texas in San Marcos. Her teaching pay helped hold the Russell family up. Winnie wrote that a calf or pig named as a child’s own, with the sale money set aside for that child, may have helped pay her way. Lillian kept studying, and earned a degree from McNeese in 1954. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 80–83, 98–107

sections.h: Fred Graham and the Lufkin pumping unit
sections.x: The engineer. Fred Graham and the Lufkin pumping unit. Fred Graham was born in Buffalo, New York, to Scottish parents and grew up in Norfolk, Virginia. Orphaned young, he worked his way west in steps: a cattle boat to England and back, jobs along the Atlantic coast, a stint in Detroit. In San Francisco he saved a burning shop by shutting off the gas, and his boss let him work nights so he could study engineering at the University of California. He came to Texas for Hughes Tool and then went to work for Lufkin Foundry and Machine Co., where he stayed more than 20 years. He met Lillian Russell on the Ferris wheel at the Lufkin county fair, and they married on Christmas Eve 1929 at the First Christian Church parsonage in Lufkin, with a honeymoon in Galveston. Winnie wrote that whenever you see “Lufkin” on the walking beam of an oil pump anywhere in the world, you should think of her father. The record backs her up, with one correction. The foundry’s famous counterbalance crank was W. C. Trout’s invention. But Fred Graham of Lufkin has his own patent: a straight-line pumping jack, filed in 1935 and granted in 1936, assigned to Lufkin Foundry and Machine Co. The record. U.S. Patent 2,048,119 , “Straight line pumping jack.” Inventor Fred Graham, Lufkin. Assignee Lufkin Foundry & Machine Co. Filed March 28, 1935; granted July 21, 1936. See the patent. The counterbalance crank was W. C. Trout’s: patent applied for in 1925 and issued in 1926. The first Lufkin pumping unit went to work on a Humble Oil well in 1923. Sources: Google Patents, US2048119A; Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 117–119; Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 112–123

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.h: Growing up a foundry engineer’s daughter
sections.x: 1930s Lufkin. Growing up a foundry engineer’s daughter. Before he ever got to Texas, Fred had lost his savings in an Iowa bank failure and worked in Detroit, as he liked to say, as an “industrial spy” on headlight magnetos. When he married Lillian, Winnie wrote, he gained 64 first cousins. Winnie grew up in Lufkin. She walked to the Coca-Cola plant to watch the bottles go by the window and gazed at the big houses on Raguet Street that sawmill fortunes built. Fred and Lillian golfed at the country club (Lillian placed in tournaments) and bowled, and Lillian belonged to the church fellowship, a book club, the garden club and a bridge club. Hard times. In the Depression a man could earn a dollar a day splitting railroad ties. Country folks sold their produce door to door in Lufkin, musicians strolled the streets, and hobos got fed on the back stoop. Aunt Addie said the Depression didn’t change much for them: they’d always been poor and grew everything they ate. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 26, 112–125. Trips. A tourist cabin at Rockport. Houston’s Rice Hotel cafeteria and Foley’s. Easter eggs hidden on the bank by the Neches River bridge on the way to Tyler County, and Sunday visits out to Grandma and Grandpa’s near Huntington. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 124–139. Christmas 1939. The whole family gathered in front of Fred and Lillian’s Lufkin house for a picture: Grandma and Grandpa Russell, Aunt Mary and Uncle Kyle, Uncle Dale and Aunt Jewel, and the children. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), p. 185

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.x: Summers at Oak Flat. Barefoot from spring to November. Summers meant Oak Flat: plowing, picking black-eyed peas, digging sweet potatoes, and swimming in the stock tank after checking it for water moccasins. Children went barefoot from spring until November and played with cornhusk dolls and paper dolls cut from the Sears catalog. A peddler came through the settlement every week. Aunt Addie and Uncle Jack. Winnie rode her horse Nellie over to their place. They slept on goose-down mattresses, and once found a rattlesnake coiled in the bedsprings. Aunt Addie lived to 91 and Uncle Jack to 89, and they died within months of each other in 1968. In her last house Aunt Addie decorated a lilac that wouldn’t bloom with lilac pictures cut from a catalog. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 152–177. The Pine Grove. A few acres of big pines on a slope beside the road from Huntington to Oak Flat, the ground soft with pine straw. It was the family’s picnic spot. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), ch. 19. Grandma Wade’s ride. In her 80s, Grandma Wade rode on the back of a grandson’s motorcycle, a German Army machine he’d brought home from the war. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 178–188. Leah’s ride. As a teenager, Grandma Leah forded a flooded creek on horseback rather than miss a social. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 60–69. Grandpa and the boar. Out in the open-range woods a wild boar once went after Grandpa, and his dog saved him. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 24–25. Lillian’s letters. Lillian kept a packet of Fred’s love letters and the gifts he gave her. When Winnie wrote the book, she and her brothers still had them. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 112–123

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.x: Huntington people. Aunts, uncles and the town. Winnie’s aunts and uncles show up all over Huntington’s history. Here’s who they were, as she remembered them. Grandpa’s brother Uncle Bud, lumberman. Earl Jackson Russell started logging as a teenager, became a lumber inspector across the Southern timber belt, worked for the Southern Pine Association in Washington, D.C., through World War II, logged mahogany in Honduras, and came home to Oak Flat in the mid-1950s. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 28–41. Grandpa’s brother Uncle Thedford, constable. Thedford Russell served several terms as constable in Huntington. He and his brother Jimmy hand-dug a well with shovels, buckets, a rope and a pulley. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 164–177. Lillian’s sister Aunt Mary, Mary’s Place. Mary Katherine worked local cafés, ran the bus station café, and then had her own: Mary’s Place in Huntington. Her husband Kyle drove road-crew bulldozers and served as a Forest Service fire-tower lookout. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 124–139. Grandpa’s sister’s husband Uncle Josh, stationmaster. Trains stopped at Huntington from the early 1900s until after World War II to load cotton bales and cattle and unload groceries. Winnie remembered Uncle Josh as the stationmaster, living in the railroad’s mustard-yellow house across a lane from the depot. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 159–160. Grandma Wade’s son-in-law Uncle Merrill, the doctor. Dr. Merrill Rogers doctored through the 1918 flu and was often paid in eggs, sweet potatoes and quilt tops. One family paid him with a fine concert violin. He traded it to Grandpa Eli for two hams at hog killing, “the violin became a fiddle,” and it stayed in the family. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 70–83, 124–139. The neighbors Oak Flat’s music. Aunt Winnie played piano for silent movies. Uncle Jack’s “Sally Goodin” could be heard at the far end of the cornfield. Instead of dances, young folks played singing games like “Skip to My Lou.”. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 138–151

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.x: 1940s. The war years. In World War II, Lufkin Foundry put up chain-link fences and guardhouses and went to war work alongside its pumping units. Workers wore photo badges. Young Winnie had a badge of her own and a little drafting table next to her father’s. The Angelina National Forest ran right up against part of Grandpa Eli’s cornfield. In 1944 the Army opened a prisoner of war camp at the Lufkin fairgrounds, and German prisoners were put to work salvaging timber. Winnie remembered farmers visiting with prisoners across the fence while they worked the woods next to Grandpa’s corn. Then came what Winnie called the Great Dispersal: families leaving the Piney Woods for war jobs on the coast. The Grahams went to Houston, Corpus Christi and Lake Charles. Grandpa couldn’t find corn seed at home in the war years, so Lillian bought it at a Houston seed store and sent it back. Many families came home again. Some made their last trip home to Jonesville Cemetery. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 178–188; Texas Historical Commission marker 13709, “German POWs in the East Texas Timber Industry” (2006): Camp No. 2 at the county fairgrounds, late April to September 1944, 500 prisoners salvaging ice-damaged timber, via the Texas Historic Sites Atlas

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.h: Jonesville Cemetery and the stone log
sections.x: Where they rest. Jonesville Cemetery and the stone log. Jonesville, about three miles southeast of Huntington, was Angelina County’s seat of government from 1854 to 1858. The town is gone. The cemetery isn’t. James Eason Russell (1824–1903) and Caroline Welch Russell (1826–1894), Grandpa Bill’s parents, are buried there. Their marker is a petrified log. Uncle “Dock” found it in the woods and had it hauled to the cemetery by log cart, and it lies across the head of both graves. Winnie called it the most prominent marker in the cemetery. Grandpa Eli and Grandma Leah lie there side by side, and Grandma Wade is there too. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 28–30, 189–191; Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 143–144, 277–278. Every family cemetery in these woods sits on ground somebody else may one day want for a pipeline, a reservoir or a plant site. Graves have been moved for Sam Rayburn Reservoir, and one pioneer family cemetery ended up inside a pipeline pump station. See Lost to the lake and the old cemeteries

sections.t: Under the black gum tree: an Oak Flat family
sections.x: Family treasures. What the family kept. Winnie wrote about the things that came down through the family. If your family has old things like these, the stories behind them are worth writing down while somebody still knows them. The amber glass shoe. A neighbor brought little Leah a tiny button-and-daisy glass shoe full of candy. Lillian later slipped it on each new baby’s foot. The hymnal. Grandma Leah’s 1947 Pentecostal Praise Hymnal , 65 cents, printed in shape notes. The family funeral hymn was “When They Ring the Golden Bells.”. The memory books. Lillian’s school memory book, filled to the back cover with friends’ verses, and her 1919 Spanish textbook. The mattress needles. Grandpa kept the needles from the New Deal cotton mattress program in a leather case under the eaves of the gal’ry. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 61–67, 98–107, 140–149

sections.t: For family researchers: Angelina County genealogy
sections.h: Where Angelina County’s family records are
sections.x: Start here. Where Angelina County’s family records are. Most of what you need is closer than you think. Here’s the path we’d take, in order. Kurth Memorial Library, Lufkin: the Ora McMullen Genealogy Room. The county history calls it one of the most complete genealogy rooms in East Texas. Ask for three things: the countywide listing of every cemetery and its marked graves; the pioneer collection, which holds every family sketch submitted for the 1976 county history, including the ones that never made it into print; and the 1974–76 history committee’s research files. Source: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. vii, 86, 247, 317. The books. Land of the Little Angel (1976), especially Chapter 16, “Some Pioneer Sketches,” and its index. R. W. Haltom’s History and Description of Angelina County (1888; reprinted 1969), the first county history. Effie Boon’s 1937 University of Texas thesis, The History of Angelina County , which is free to read online and lists the old-timers she interviewed in 1934. Archie Birdsong Mathews’s 1952 UT thesis on the county’s economic development. Source: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 62, 151, 205, 320–322. Old newspapers. Early issues of the Lufkin Daily News and The Lufkin News are searchable for free on the Portal to Texas History. In Huntington, the McMullen Memorial Library is worth asking about the old Angelina County News (1939–50) and Huntington-Zavalla Herald. Courthouse records. The Angelina County Clerk and District Clerk hold deeds, probate and court records back to 1846. The county history notes records from the Homer years survive at the Lufkin courthouse. Source: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 213, 320. Confederate service and pensions. The Texas State Library and Archives keeps the index of Confederate pension applications, including widows’ pensions. The National Park Service’s Soldiers and Sailors database lists units. The county raised Company D of the 7th Texas Cavalry in 1861 and a second company at Homer in 1862. Land grants and surveys. The Texas General Land Office holds the original Spanish, Mexican and Republic land grants. The county’s first surveyor, William G. Lang, made its first land map in 1848. Source: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 22, 281. Graves and markers. Find a Grave and the Texas Historical Commission’s Historic Sites Atlas cover many county cemeteries. Then go walk them, before the next road or pipeline does

sections.t: For family researchers: Angelina County genealogy
sections.h: Pioneer families in Land of the Little Angel
sections.x: Is your family in the book? Pioneer families in Land of the Little Angel. Chapter 16 of the 1976 county history profiles the families who settled here before about 1910; we list 138 of them. Type a surname to check. Page numbers point you to where that family’s sketch falls in the book. The committee itself warned that the sketches, sent in by families, contain errors, so treat them as leads and check them against records. Search surnames. Outlined in red: our founder’s lines. Some surnames appear in other families’ sketches too (Russell daughters married into the Aldredge and Atkinson families, for example), so check the book’s index as well. To see everywhere a name shows up on this site, try Find your family. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), Chapter 16, pp. 247–315

sections.t: For family researchers: Angelina County genealogy
sections.x: Walk the ground. Old cemeteries of the county. Most of the county’s first cemeteries began beside churches in the 1860s and 1870s. Others started when a family buried someone on their own land and later gave the ground. So many early graves are unmarked that nobody can say for sure which cemetery is oldest. Walker Cemetery Redland, about 1855. Named for Thomas R. Walker. Prairie Grove Near Diboll. Begun in 1849 with the graves of three Stovall children. Bodan Cemetery Pollok, 1850s. It straddles the old Smuggler’s Trail. Homer Cemetery 1860s, at the old county seat. Largent Cemetery Near Bethlehem, 1862. Page Cemetery Near Manning, 1863. Jonesville Cemetery About three miles southeast of Huntington, at the second county seat. Home of the petrified-log marker. Center Cemetery Near Huntington and the Rocky Springs community. Old Center About eight miles southeast of Lufkin, early 1880s. The Havard cemeteries Family cemeteries of the Havard brothers; two near Saron date to the early 1870s. Renfro Cemetery On the old Renfro homeplace, Renfro Prairie (Beulah). John Folkner Renfro’s grave. Gann Cemetery At Clawson. Not every grave stayed put. Before Sam Rayburn Reservoir filled, families’ graves were dug up and moved, seven cemeteries from Concord alone. And the county history records a pioneer family, the Brazils, buried in a cemetery that ended up inside the Gulf pipeline pump station at Redland. Unmarked family cemeteries are the most at risk when land changes hands. If you know of one, write it down and tell us. See Lost to the lake. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 85–86, 173, 255, 264, 273, 277, 299, 304–305, 309. The Texas Historical Commission marker at the old Fastrill logging camp, dedicated in April 2000. Photo by Jonathan Gerland. Markers like this often hold the best short history of a place. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas

sections.t: For family researchers: Angelina County genealogy
sections.x: Our founder’s lines. Her mother’s side runs through Oak Flat and Huntington. Her father’s side, the Fosters, came from Alto in Cherokee County, and her grandfather spent his working life on the railroads that tied the Piney Woods together. Huntington The Snowdens. Hardy and Nettie Snowden, “Big Papa” and “Big Mama,” with their son George, his wife Rosa and a grandson. Family photo. Hardy Alexander Snowden and Nettie Gardner Snowden raised a big family at Huntington. Hardy died there in 1949 and Nettie in 1952. Their daughter Stella married Randolph Forrest, and Stella’s daughter Jewell married Dale Russell of Oak Flat. Vernice Snowden, George and Rosa’s little girl, at Huntington in the early 1920s. Family photo. Thelma Forrest, Stella’s daughter, as a baby in the early 1920s. Family photo. Sources: family records and photographs. Alto, Lufkin and Diboll Charles Henry Foster, railroad man. Charles Henry Foster with his firstborn, about 1950. Family photo. Charles Henry Foster was born Sept. 19, 1928, in Alto, to Nesbitt E. and Rosa Neely Foster, and grew up in the Primrose community. He graduated from Alto High School in 1946, served with the Army of occupation in Japan, went to Pineywoods Business College, and went to work for the Southern Pacific Railroad in Lufkin. He later worked for the Texas South-Eastern Railroad in Diboll, the Temple family’s line out of Diboll. He married Mary Elizabeth Barfield, and he died in Lufkin on April 24, 2010. Sources: obituary, Cherokeean Herald (Rusk), April 28, 2010, p. 4 ; family records. Oak Flat and Homer The Chestnuts. Alfred Chestnut (1798–1864) was born on Six Run Creek in Sampson County, North Carolina. He and his wife, Mary Jane Campbell Chestnut (1818–1879), were living near Homer by the late 1850s. Alfred died at Oak Flat in 1864 and Mary Jane at Homer in 1879, and both are buried at Oak Flat. Their daughter Mary (1852–1913) married W. D. “Bill” Russell. She’s our founder’s 3rd great-grandmother. Sources: family records. Ora, near Huntington The Herringtons and Cochrans. James Herrington (1825–1889), born in Alabama, married Catharine Cochran (1833–1903), daughter of Joshua Butler Cochran of Ora, and they raised a big family near Huntington. Their daughter Jo Ann (1858–1890) married J. H. McClure. She’s our founder’s 4th great-grandmother. James, Catharine and Jo Ann are buried in the Herrington Cemetery near Huntington, the same family cemetery as Joseph Herrington, the county’s first chief justice. Sources: family records; Herrington Cemetery survey (Debra Coursey Pitts and D. J. Pitts, 2002, USGenWeb Archives); Texas Historical Commission marker 7003. Our founder’s father Mary and Bobby Foster. Mary Barfield Foster holding her son Bobby, 1959. Family photo. Mary Elizabeth Barfield Foster was born in Logansport, Louisiana, in 1928 and died in Alto in 2005. Her son Robert Merrell “Bobby” Foster (1959–1988) was born in Lufkin. He was our founder’s father. Bobby Foster as a baby, 1959. Family photo. Sources: family records and photographs. The Renfros, Forrests, Snowdens, Russells, Chestnuts, Herringtons and Fosters. Our founder, Fawn Elizabeth Zion, descends from families in both books: the Renfros of Renfro Prairie, who came in 1840 and started one of the county’s first schools; the Forrests of Huntington; and the Russells, including W. D. “Bill” Russell, the county’s last Confederate veteran, and her grandfather Hayden Russell, who played on Lufkin’s 1957 PONY League world champions. East Texas Legacy Coalition. Hometown Huntington. Before the town, there was Renfro Prairie and the farms around it. Then the railroad came through, and Huntington was laid out in a single summer

1840 Renfro Prairie. Renfro Prairie, near present-day Huntington, takes its name from the Renfro family, who settled there around 1840. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976)

1880s The town that almost was. Before Huntington, there was Ora, between today’s town and the Angelina River. Ora had a school district by 1880 and, people said, the county’s first schoolhouse built of sawed lumber. Its postmaster named the post office in 1884 for his baby daughter, Ora Medford. When the railroad town came along, Ora’s families moved to it, and Ora’s school became the seed of Huntington’s. In the late 1880s Lewis Baird and Alvin Russell tried to start a town about a mile east of where Huntington stands, near where the T&NO and Cotton Belt lines would later cross. It didn’t take. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 56–57, 163, 178, 293

sections.h: Lots sold to the highest bidder
sections.x: 1900 Lots sold to the highest bidder. The Texas & New Orleans line came through, and promoters E. A. Blount and W. J. Townsend filed a plat in June 1900. On June 22 they auctioned the lots. Hundreds of buyers came, and the county history says there was plenty of liquor and a few fistfights by the tracks. The post office opened July 23, 1900, with Capt. R. D. Chapman as postmaster. The town is named for C. P. Huntington, chairman of the Southern Pacific railroad. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976)

sections.h: Saloons, a lodge and two churches
sections.x: 1900–1902 Saloons, a lodge and two churches. Capt. R. D. Chapman, the first postmaster, ran a big general store, a piling and tie company and the undertaking business; the county history calls him the father of Huntington. Dr. C. B. Stewart was the first doctor, and his son Ray, born in 1901, was the first boy born in the new townsite. Before Prohibition the new town had seven saloons. In 1901 Homer’s Masonic Lodge No. 254, the county’s first lodge, chartered in 1861, moved to Huntington. That same year First Baptist Church was organized under a brush arbor, and the Methodists started meeting in a store building in 1902. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 69, 75, 87–88, 164, 304

1900–1959 Schools on Renfro land. Huntington’s first school opened in 1900 on the site of the Renfro home, across the street from today’s school. From 1903 to 1913 it ran on John F. Renfro’s property. A two-story brick school followed in 1914, and the first 11th-grade class in 1921. From 1939 to 1959 the district was the Huntington Rural Schools, gathering in the country schools around it: Oak Flat, Odell, Rocky Hill, Salem, Ora and more. John F. Renfro, the Renfro Prairie pioneer’s grandson, went on to the Texas House from 1927 to 1931. Read the Renfro story. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 35, 56–57, 299

1907–1940s A railroad town. In 1907 a short logging line, the Shreveport, Houston & Gulf, ran from the Carter-Kelley mill at Manning to Huntington. It quit in the 1930s after the mill burned. In 1917 the new state forestry department put one of its five district headquarters in Huntington. Winnie Graham remembered trains stopping at Huntington until after World War II to load cotton bales and cattle and unload groceries, and the stationmaster’s mustard-yellow house across a lane from the depot. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 139, 173, 188–189; Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 159–160. The railroad bridge over the Neches at Rockland. The old East Texas Railroad stopped on the south bank here until Southern Pacific bought it, made it the Texas & New Orleans and built it north through Huntington. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas

1900–1940s A railroad and cotton town. Huntington got telephones in 1907 and electricity in 1927, and incorporated in 1937 with Fowler Burris as its first mayor. By the 1940s it had about 1,000 people, three electric cotton gins and what one local called the largest cotton market in the county. Raymond Tatum of Huntington served two terms in the Texas House, 1949–52. In 1937 a 100-acre palmetto brake grew along Stanley Creek, eight miles east of town. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 19, 35, 164–165

1917–1976 Fire watch and cane syrup. In 1917, when the state’s new forestry department split East Texas into five fire districts, one was headquartered in Huntington. By 1925 the county had three forest patrolmen, at Huntington, Pollok and Zavalla. And in 1976 the county history named B. W. Horton of Huntington among the last people in the county still making cane syrup. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 10, 188–189

sections.h: A library for the men who didn’t come home
sections.x: 1953 A library for the men who didn’t come home. McMullen Memorial Library was dedicated June 21, 1953, in memory of 19 Huntington-area men who died in World War II. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976)

1918–1974 A sports town. Huntington’s early boys’ teams were coached around 1918–22 by a woman, Charlie B. Adams. Annie Lee Jones coached the first girls’ team in 1929–30. The county history lists state titles in 1959, 1960, 1962 and 1974. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976)

1911–1972 Huntington’s newspapers. Casper Ricks started the Huntington Herald in 1911. George J. Ivy’s Huntington Messenger came in 1920, the Huntington Weekly News in 1928, and in 1939 J. W. Cloud renamed it the Angelina County News. In 1972 Buddy and Jeanie Moore started the Huntington-Zavalla Herald. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 208–209

1950 A newspaper fire. J. W. and Josie Cloud ran the Angelina County News in Huntington from 1939. In March 1950, a fire the county history calls mysterious destroyed their office and printing plant. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976)

Our people From the founder’s own family. Fawn Elizabeth Zion, who started the East Texas Legacy Coalition, has roots that run deep in this ground. Her people show up all through the county’s own history book. Her family’s Oak Flat story, from Winnie Graham’s memoir, is on Under the black gum tree. Great-great-great-grandfather 1942. W. D. “Bill” Russell. Born in Dallas County, Arkansas, in 1848, he came to Texas as a little boy of five and enlisted in the Confederate Army at Galveston. When he died in 1942, he was Angelina County’s last surviving Confederate veteran. He’s buried at Jonesville Cemetery near Huntington. Grandfather 1957. Hayden Russell. W. D.’s great-grandson, born the year W. D. died. Hayden played on the 1957 Lufkin PONY League All-Stars, the team that won the PONY League World Series, beating Maywood, Illinois, 5–2 in the final. The founder’s family 1904. The Forrests of Huntington. Dr. Robert B. Forrest came to Huntington in 1904 to practice medicine and became president of Huntington Guaranty State Bank. Forrests were here before the town: Anthony Forrest died near Huntington in the 1880s. The county history also records George W. Forrest’s marriage to Josephine Jones, and their daughter Ida’s to Otto Foster. W. D. Russell’s brothers 1900. Joseph and Albion Russell. Joseph Gray Russell (1851–1901) was postmaster at Ora, between Huntington and the Angelina River, in 1900. His brother Albion Brown Russell (1854–1936) married Lizzie Stovall and raised seven children; he died at Huntington. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 178, 246, 267, 290, 300, 304; family records; PONY Baseball, list of World Series champions (1957: Lufkin, Texas, 5–2 over Maywood, Ill.). About our sources. Much of this page comes from Land of the Little Angel , the 1976 county history edited by Bob Bowman. We retell it in our own words and point you to the book; we don’t reprint it. Kurth Memorial Library in Lufkin keeps a copy. Know something we got wrong, or have a family story that belongs here? Write contact@grailsystems.io. Got old Huntington photos? Send them with who, where and when. We’ll ask before we post, and credit your family

Folkways of the Piney Woods How we used to do. Riding the ring, party lines, dog-trot houses, cane syrup boiled in a wash pot, a rose plowed around in the middle of a cornfield. The everyday ways of Deep East Texas, from the families who lived them. Schoolchildren on a circular swing, San Augustine, 1938. Russell Lee, Farm Security Administration. Library of Congress

The old tournament. Riding the Ring. Picture a Saturday in the late 1800s. A row of posts stands in a field, each with an iron ring hanging from an arm. A young man comes down the course at a full gallop with a long wooden pole and tries to spear every ring. The one who takes the most rings gets to choose the lady he honors. East Texans called it Riding the Ring. Texans held these ring tournaments after the Civil War, often with a barbecue and a dance, and they were modeled on the jousting tournaments of the Middle Ages. Winnie Graham’s grandfather, Eli Russell of Oak Flat, won one. Then he gave his prize to a different girl than the one he’d marry, which made Leah jealous. Where it comes from. Winnie’s college sources traced the sport back to medieval jousting. A 1994 genealogical journal remembers tournaments in Live Oak, Atascosa, Wilson, Jefferson, Leon and Montgomery counties, and notes J. Frank Dobie rode in them as a young man. San Antonio’s Texas Cavaliers, formed in 1926, revived the tradition. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 73–75; Fount Rambie, “Tournaments,” Stirpes 34, no. 1 (March 1994), p. 70, via the Portal to Texas History

Say it right. Piney Woods talk. Winnie heard the old Piney Woods speech from a great-grandfather born in 1848 and wrote it down before it disappeared. Some of it you’ll still hear at the feed store. Some of it you won’t hear anywhere anymore. vittles. Food. mought. Might. hope. The old past tense of help. fellers. Fellows, men, boys. kids. Baby goats first. Children second. blinky milk. Milk just starting to turn. surp. Cane syrup, the kind boiled down at home. Not molasses. gal’ry. The gallery: the big front porch, the summer living room. chimlee. Chimney. fahr. Fire. “Put another back stick on the fahr.”. back stick. The big log laid at the back of the fireplace to throw the heat forward. wahr. Wire. “Bob wahr” is barbed wire. play pretties. Toys: cornhusk dolls, paper dolls cut from the Sears catalog. Blue Norther. A hard, sudden cold front that drops the temperature in an hour. do like they do across the river. Do without. ting-a-lings. Tangerines, in one Oak Flat family, after a neighbor’s way of saying it. saucered and blowed. Hot coffee poured into the saucer and blown on to cool it. Farture Fumers. Grandpa Eli’s joke name for the Future Farmers. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 18–20, 71, 84–97, 107, 128, 152–158

sections.h: Dog-trots, gal’ries and the party line
sections.x: House and home. Dog-trots, gal’ries and the party line. The dog-trot house was the Piney Woods answer to summer: two log rooms under one roof with an open hall down the middle for the breeze (and the dogs) to pass through. Winnie wrote that they once numbered in the thousands in East Texas. The front gal’ry was the summer living room, with a washstand, cane-bottom chairs and a porch swing. The fireplace. A mud-and-stick “chimlee” and a big back stick to throw the heat into the room. Cooking, warmth and light all came from the same hearth. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 152–158. The party line. One wire ran from the Huntington telephone office out to Oak Flat on trees and fence posts. Everybody shared it and every house had its own ring: Grandpa’s was two shorts. There was no ground wire, so you drove your own rod, and when a call got faint somebody hollered to go pour a dipper of water on the ground wahr. Telephones reached Oak Flat about 35 years before electricity did. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 150–151. Getting the lights. Electricity didn’t reach Oak Flat until the 1950s. The first family with a refrigerator gave away ice to the neighbors. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 18–20, 84–97. The cotton mattress program. During the New Deal, farmers were given needles and free ticking to sew mattresses out of cotton they couldn’t sell. At Oak Flat they made them at the old church house. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 148–149. Radio nights. A battery radio, charged at a garage in town. At noon, the local news and the sick list. On Saturday night, the Grand Ole Opry and the Louisiana Hayride , and the Light Crust Doughboys out of Fort Worth. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 152–158. Washday. A three-legged cast-iron wash pot over a fire, homemade lye soap and a washboard. The same kind of pot boiled down the cane syrup. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 87–88, 98

sections.h: Open range, ox teams and martin houses
sections.x: Field and woods. Open range, ox teams and martin houses. Until about the 1950s much of these woods was open range. Hogs ran loose and fattened on mast, the acorns and nuts on the forest floor, and every family registered its own earmark, a pattern of notches cut in the ear, so they could tell whose hog was whose. Folks picked wild berries for jelly and cobbler and robbed wild bee trees for honey. Driving oxen. A team had a near ox and an off ox. “Whoa, come ‘ere” turned them left. “Yea, back” turned them right. Timber wagons ran with up to four pairs. Winnie said the old plows stayed in use until after World War II. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 18–20, 71–72. Hog killing. It waited for the first frosty morning. The meat was smoked over hickory and some of it canned. Sweet potatoes went into the potato house for the winter. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 84–97. Purple martins. Most farmsteads had a martin house up on a tall pole. Grandpa Eli built them twelve rooms at a time. The martins ate flying insects. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), p. 169. Contour rows. County agricultural agents helped farmers lay their fields out in contours and terraces to keep the soil and the rain from washing away. Grandpa grew watermelons on his. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), p. 164. A calf for college. An old custom: name a calf or a pig as one child’s own, and when it sold, the money went to that child’s needs. Winnie thought that’s how her mother got to college. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 98–107. Picking cotton. Cotton was king here until about World War II, then cattle. Pickers were paid a few cents a pound, and a hundred pounds was a good day. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 9–11, 98–107. Those contour rows were water conservation. After World War II, the county’s landowners organized a soil conservation district because, in the county history’s words, the topsoil was washing off their farms. Caring for the land and the water has always been part of farming here. See Our water has a paper trail. Pauline Durham and Elmer Ray Wells on Baalam the mule at Fastrill, about 1928. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas

sections.h: Cornbread every day, light bread on Sunday
sections.x: The kitchen. Cornbread every day, light bread on Sunday. Cornbread was the daily bread, and it had better be brown on top. Store-bought wheat “light bread” was an extravagance, and flour mostly went into breakfast biscuits. Dinner was at noon; supper was whatever was left, cold. Buttermilk was the everyday drink, and if company asked for sweet milk, they asked politely. Mayhaws in a skiff. Mayhaws grow in the soggy creek and river bottoms. In a good mayhaw year the bottoms flooded, the ripe fruit fell and floated, and a few folks rowed skiffs into the swamp to scoop it up and sell it. It makes the finest jelly there is. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 88–89. Mayhaw jelly recipe Surp, not molasses. Families pressed their own cane in hand-turned mills and boiled the juice down in iron wash pots. That was syrup. Molasses was what the big sugar mills left over. Syrup and biscuits were supposed to come out even. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 87–88. Bitter milk. When the cows got into bitterweed, the milk and butter turned so bitter the cats wouldn’t touch it. You could taste the pasture in the churn. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), p. 88. Wild berries. Blackberries, dewberries, the rare huckleberry, and muscadines so tart they puckered your mouth but made a fine jelly. Pawpaws, and wild strawberries no bigger than a pea. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 88–89, 143–144. Our wild foods guide Coffee. Boiled, then saucered and blowed. In the Civil War, when there wasn’t any, folks parched sweet potatoes, beans and corn and ground them for a stand-in. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 84–97; Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 30. Summer treats. Banana pudding with real custard and vanilla wafers. Watermelons kept cool under the bed. Peanuts curing in the back room, and children sneaking raw goobers out of the pile. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 152–158. Through the year. Roasting ears and creamed corn, black-eyed peas or butterbeans with a piece of pork, okra, creek perch rolled in cornmeal and fried, a rooster penned and fed grain before Sunday dinner, winter greens, and Irish potatoes planted in late winter. School lunch went in a syrup bucket. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 84–97; Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), p. 41. Sweet gum gum. Children chewed the sap of the sweet gum tree like chewing gum. Winnie said it tasted good and left a gooey mess on your teeth. Sources: Winnie Graham, Listening to Plants: A Pathway to New Uses (2020), p. 7

sections.h: Shape notes, play parties and the fiddle
sections.x: Singing. Shape notes, play parties and the fiddle. Country churches sang out of shape-note hymnals, where each note of the scale has its own shape so a congregation could read music without lessons. It’s an American way of teaching singing that goes back to about 1800. Grandma Leah’s was the 1947 Pentecostal Praise Hymnal , and it cost 65 cents. Instead of dances, young people had play parties: singing games like “Skip to My Lou” and “Pickin’ Up Paw-Paws.” The fiddle still got played. At Oak Flat, Uncle Jack’s “Sally Goodin” carried to the far end of the cornfield. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 138–151

Signs and sayings. What the old folks knew. Old house places. You can still find abandoned homesteads deep in the woods by the patches of jonquils and the scraggly rose bushes somebody planted by the door. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), p. 165. Planting peas. Plant your black-eyed peas when the fishermen start sitting down on the creek bank, about April. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), pp. 164–177. Catalpa worms. The caterpillars that strip a catalpa tree, the “catawba worms,” made the best fish bait going. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), p. 175. Christmas green. Country folks hung a sprig of yaupon, with its red winter berries, for Christmas. Look, don’t eat: the berries will make you sick. Sources: Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods (Nacogdoches: Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013), p. 137. Rain crows and whip-poor-wills. The “rain crow,” the yellow-billed cuckoo, called before a rain, and the whip-poor-will’s call meant spring had come. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 19–20

Please read. A word on safety. This page is history, not instructions. The old families doctored with whatever they had, and some of it was dangerous. We don’t share home remedies. If you put up food, follow the current USDA home canning guidance: low-acid foods like peas, beans and meat need a pressure canner. Never eat a wild plant you can’t identify for certain. Poison help: 1-800-222-1222. It also sits on top of a community, family farms and graves. Here’s what the county history remembers about what went under the water

sections.h: Concord: a hundred years, then gone
sections.x: 1860–1960 Concord: a hundred years, then gone. Concord grew up around a small plank church in 1860. About a hundred years later, the reservoir took it. The county history says every one of its more than 100 residents had to leave, and seven cemeteries were moved. Its school district was folded into Zavalla. A log cabin that belonged to Col. T. L. Mott had to be bought back from the Corps of Engineers and moved about 12 miles, to Jasper County, to save it. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976)

1950s–1960s Farms and family land. The book’s family sketches keep mentioning the lake: land of the Moore and Cochran families, McGilbery Lake where Cornelius McGilbery settled, and the Sumrall family, whose graves were dug up from Parker Cemetery and reburied at Concord before the water came. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976)

Still today Graves that didn’t move. Moved cemeteries don’t always move every grave. The county history notes unmarked graves in more than one place, and one pioneer family cemetery that ended up inside a pipeline pump station near Redland. Federal relocation records could show which graves were moved and which were left behind. Those records can be requested. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976)

Now Why we tell this. Big water projects get sold as progress, and some of them are. But somebody always pays, and it’s usually the people who were already here. When the next project comes, the families in its path deserve to know first, and to have a say. The lake has darker stories too. In 1973, police dug in the woods near Rayburn for the victims of Houston’s Candy Man. The Candy Man and the lake. If your family was moved for Rayburn, we’d like to hear from you: contact@grailsystems.io. We’ll ask before we post anything. Sources: Your stories. About our sources. sections.t: The Candy Man and the lake
sections.h: The candy man of the Heights
sections.x: 1960s The candy man of the Heights. Dean Corll grew up partly in Southeast Texas. He graduated from Vidor High School, near Beaumont, then settled in Houston. His mother ran a small candy business that became the Corll Candy Company, in a bungalow on West 22nd Street in the Houston Heights, directly across from Helms Elementary School. It closed in June 1968. Neighborhood kids knew him as the friendly man from the candy factory who handed out free sweets. That’s where the name came from. To the neighbors, he was a polite man who liked kids. Sources: Dean Corll (Wikipedia, with its cited sources) ; “The Lost Boys,” Texas Monthly ; “Houston’s Darkest Hours,” Houstonia ; Houston Chronicle (a neighbor’s description)

sections.t: The Candy Man and the lake
sections.x: 1970–1973 Boys who didn’t come home. Over three years, teenage boys kept disappearing from the Heights and nearby. Many of the boys had gone to the same junior high. Corll paid two teenagers from the neighborhood, David Owen Brooks and Elmer Wayne Henley, to bring him boys with offers of parties and rides. We won’t describe what happened to them after that. Their families have lived with it long enough. Sources: Texas Monthly ; National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, 2023

sections.t: The Candy Man and the lake
sections.x: Aug. 8, 1973 The morning it ended. Early that morning at Corll’s house at 2020 Lamar Drive in Pasadena, 17-year-old Wayne Henley shot him dead. Henley said Corll had threatened him and two other teenagers who had come over for a party. Then Henley called the police himself and started talking. He and Brooks led officers to three burial grounds: a rented boat shed in southwest Houston, the beach at High Island on the Gulf, and the woods of our own corner of East Texas. Sources: Wikipedia ; CBS News ; TIME, 1973

sections.t: The Candy Man and the lake
sections.x: Aug. 1973 What was buried at Rayburn. Corll’s family had a cabin by Lake Sam Rayburn. In the woods near it, in San Augustine County, Henley and Brooks showed deputies where four boys were buried. TIME reported the site was about 150 miles northeast of Houston. Brooks later admitted that one morning he and Henley went fishing at the lake before burying a boy there. People came to Rayburn for the fishing. Some of them never knew what was out in the pines. The four boys found near Rayburn were: William “Billy” Ray Lawrence 15. Raymond Stanley Blackburn 20. Homer Louis Garcia 15. Michael Anthony Baulch 15. All four disappeared in the summer of 1973, the last summer of it. Sources: KPRC, 2021 (San Augustine, four bodies); TIME, 1973 ; Texas Monthly (Brooks’s confession); Wikipedia (names, ages, burial sites)

sections.t: The Candy Man and the lake
sections.x: Still open The boy with no name. More than fifty years later, one of the boys has never been identified. He was found Aug. 9, 1973, was about 15 to 18 years old, and had likely been dead a year or more. In 2023 the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children released a new image of what he may have looked like, hoping someone would know him. ML73-3356. If you know anything, or you think a missing uncle, cousin or classmate from the early ’70s could be him, contact the Harris County Institute of Forensic Sciences and give the case number ML73-3356 , or call NCMEC at 1-800-THE-LOST. See his NCMEC poster and the new image →. That’s the part of this story that East Texans can still help finish. Somebody’s family is still waiting. Sources: NCMEC poster ; ABC13, Aug. 7, 2023 ; KPRC, 2022

sections.t: The Candy Man and the lake
sections.x: After What became of the rest. Henley was convicted of six of the murders and is serving life in a Texas prison; he was denied parole again in November 2025. Brooks was convicted of one murder, Billy Lawrence’s, sentenced to life, and died in custody in 2020. The Pasadena house was torn down in 2023. Searchers have gone back to the old sites more than once, looking for boys who were never found. Sources: Wikipedia ; ABC13, Texas EquuSearch search ; Yahoo News, 2023 (house razed)
