East Texas Legacy Coalition. The ones who stood up for this place. Heroes in Deep East Texas don’t usually get statues. They get a road named after them, or a patch of woods that’s still standing because they wouldn’t let it go. Here are some of the people who looked after our land and water before it was our turn

1912–2007 Born in Karnack, Harrison County. Lady Bird Johnson. Lady Bird Johnson among bluebonnets and Indian paintbrush, Central Texas, 1968. Photo by Robert Knudsen, LBJ Presidential Library (C9479-17), public domain. Before she was a first lady, Claudia Alta Taylor was a little girl in Karnack, a crossroads town of about a hundred people near the Louisiana line. A nursemaid said she was “as purty as a lady bird,” and the name stuck for life. She grew up to run the first major legislative campaign ever led by a first lady. The Highway Beautification Act of 1965, which folks called “Lady Bird’s Bill,” went after billboards and junkyards along the new interstates. She insisted it was never just about looking pretty. In her diary she wrote that clean water, parks, pollution and poverty were all one tangled skein: “All the threads are interwoven.”. Signed into law Oct. 22, 1965: the Highway Beautification Act. 1969: started the Texas Highway Beautification Awards and paid the winners out of her own checkbook for twenty years. That’s a big reason Texas roadsides bloom with bluebonnets and paintbrush every spring. 1982, on her 70th birthday: founded the National Wildflower Research Center to protect native plants. It became the Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center in 1997 and is now part of the University of Texas. “All the threads are interwoven.” Lady Bird Johnson, diary entry, Jan. 27, 1965 Sources: LBJ Presidential Library (born Karnack, Dec. 22, 1912; the nickname); Marion County Herald (Harrison County); Vineyard Gazette obituary (Karnack, population 100); Texas House Concurrent Resolution 253 (2009) (first major legislative campaign by a first lady; “Lady Bird’s Bill”); EBSCO Research Starters (signed Oct. 22, 1965); LBJ Library biography (beautification awards, 1982 founding); LBJ Library biography as reprinted by Denton ISD (1969 start of the awards); Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center (1997 renaming, UT Austin); USPS Stamp of Approval blog (diary quote and date). See her in the wildflowers The LBJ Library’s Lady Bird Johnson page, with photos and her own home movies. Visit the Wildflower Center Austin. Her native-plant work, still going

1886–1970 Born south of Saratoga, Hardin County Lance Rosier. Photographer unknown. Courtesy National Park Service. Lance Rosier, “Mr. Big Thicket”. Lance Rosier grew up in his aunt’s boarding house in Saratoga and never had much use for hunting game or chasing a paycheck. He hunted flowers. He’d wander the Thicket for days, and with no formal schooling he came to know just about every plant in it. By the 1960s, conservationists and politicians who wanted to understand the Thicket had come to know him. He spent his life pushing to protect it from the timber and oil companies, and he died in 1970, four years before the preserve became law. The largest unit of Big Thicket National Preserve carries his name. Sources: National Park Service, “Lance Rosier” ; NPS, Lance Rosier Unit sign ; Texas Highways (largest of the preserve’s 15 units); Texas Observer, Aug. 29, 1969 (politicians and conservationists knew him). The “Bridge to Nowhere” over Little Pine Island Bayou, in the Lance Rosier Unit that carries his name. NPS photo by Scott Sharaga, via National Park Service

1964–1974 Saratoga to Washington Geraldine Watson surveying a dead cypress, 1973. Photographer unknown. Courtesy National Park Service. The neighbors who wouldn’t quit. In October 1964, local people met at the Saratoga Methodist Church and started the Big Thicket Association. Botanist Geraldine Watson, who grew up in the region, fought beside Rosier, Ned Fritz and Maxine Johnston, and later became the preserve’s plant ecologist. Senator Ralph Yarborough and Congressmen Bob Eckhardt and Charlie Wilson carried it in Washington. On Oct. 11, 1974, it became law. Ten years of meetings, letters and showing up. That’s the playbook. It still works. Sources: Big Thicket Reporter #121 (1964 founding meeting); Texas Parks & Wildlife magazine, July 2024 (Watson, Fritz, Johnston); Sierra Club Houston (Yarborough, Eckhardt, Wilson, Bentsen); NPS (signing date)

1965 Big Thicket Association. Dempsie Henley. Lance Rosier recruited him to lead the new Big Thicket Association. In 1965 Henley invited U.S. Senator Ralph Yarborough to come see the Thicket for himself, with Rosier as the guide. That trip is what persuaded Yarborough to push for protecting it in Washington. Sometimes the most important thing an advocate does is get the right person into the woods. Source: National Park Service, “Lance Rosier”

sections.h: Maxine Johnston, the godmother of the Big Thicket
sections.x: Since 1964 Batson and Beaumont. Maxine Johnston, the godmother of the Big Thicket. A librarian. She joined Lamar University’s library in 1955 and became its director in 1980. She joined the Big Thicket Association in 1964, served as its president twice, from 1972 to 1975 and from 1994 to 1998, edited its newsletters and led people on tours of the Thicket. Rosier and Geraldine Watson were her friends. She also did what librarians do best: she saved the record. At Lamar she built an archive on the Big Thicket that runs to 25 collections, and she arranged for Larry Jene Fisher’s photographs to land there. In 2024, at 95, Texas Monthly reported she was still at it. Sources: Lamar University, 2018 (1955; association since 1964; presidencies); Texas Parks & Wildlife magazine, January 2020 (director in 1980; 25 collections; “godmother”); National Parks Conservation Association (newsletters and tours); Texas Monthly (friendships with Rosier and Watson); Lamar University, Larry Jene Fisher Collection (donated by Maxine Johnston); Texas Monthly, Oct. 16, 2024 (95 and still fighting)

sections.h: Larry Jene Fisher, the man who saved the Thicket’s faces
sections.x: 1902–1950s Saratoga, Hardin County. Larry Jene Fisher, the man who saved the Thicket’s faces. An organist, aviator, playwright and filmmaker who moved to Saratoga around 1940 and lived there about 15 years. Through the 1930s and ’40s he photographed Big Thicket people living the old way: syrup mills, deer hunts, rooter hogs, railroad tie making, barrel staves. He knew that way of life was ending, and he made sure it was recorded. His photographs of the Thicket’s plants and animals helped the first push to protect it. His pictures sat neglected for nearly 50 years until a 2000 exhibit brought them back. Lamar University now holds thousands of them, and many are free to view online. See his photographs on the Portal to Texas History. Sources: Lamar University, Larry Jene Fisher Collection (born 1902; Saratoga about 15 years; role in the first preservation movement); University of Texas Press, Big Thicket People (1930s–40s folk life); Texas Co-op Power (8,000 scanned images); Texas Observer (neglected nearly 50 years; 2000 exhibit)

1729–1809 Nacogdoches. Antonio Gil Y’Barbo. When Spain ordered East Texas settlers to abandon their homes in 1773, Y’Barbo kept petitioning to bring them back. In 1779 he led them home and rebuilt Nacogdoches. Plenty of people talk about loving a place. He walked a whole town back to it. Sources: SNAC, Antonio Gil Y’Barbo records (UT Libraries; SFA East Texas Research Center); National Register nomination, Nacogdoches

1990s–2010s Victoria, Texas. Kenneth Schustereit. The San Antonio Current called him “the gender-switch Erin Brockovich.” Kenneth Schustereit was an industrial electrician and pipe fitter from Victoria with a high school diploma. He got into water the hard way: a man working on his parents’ well told him that someday he’d have to put a meter on it and pay for the water under his own land. So he started reading. He’d come to public meetings in his blue work clothes, straight off a nine-hour shift, carrying photocopies of Chapter 36 of the Texas Water Code. The state’s experts brought laptops. He brought the law. He fought “the GBRA deal,” a plan to pump 94,000 acre-feet of Guadalupe River water a year more than 130 miles uphill to San Antonio. He pushed the Texas Water Development Board to account for leaking oilfield injection wells in its groundwater models. When voters in Victoria, Lavaca, Colorado and Comal counties turned down the proposed groundwater districts in November 2001, the Victoria Advocate credited him by name. A retired civil engineer on San Antonio’s water advisory panel met with him and vouched for his facts. He was still speaking up during public comment at Guadalupe-Blanco River Authority board meetings in 2015. You don’t need a degree to read the law. You need a copy of it and the nerve to stand up. Our takeaway from his story Sources: Steve Badrich, “Bad Deal for Bad Water,” San Antonio Current, June 20, 2002 ; Guadalupe-Blanco River Authority board minutes, March 18, 2015 (public comment)

sections.h: W. Goodrich Jones, the father of Texas forestry
sections.x: 1860–1950 Temple, Texas. W. Goodrich Jones, the father of Texas forestry. A banker, not a forester. In 1898 he rode horseback across East Texas to see the timber for himself, and came back with a bleak report. In 1914 he gathered about 20 people in the Carnegie library in Temple and founded the Texas Forestry Association. A year later the Legislature created the state’s forestry department, which became the Texas Forest Service. His motto was simple: for every tree cut, plant a tree. Sources: Texas Historical Commission marker 2849 (1914 association; 1915 law); “Site of Organization of the Texas Forestry Association” marker, Temple (Carnegie library meeting); Texas A&M Forest Service presentation (1898 horseback survey); Sierra Club Houston (his motto); W. Goodrich Jones Papers, SFA East Texas Research Center

sections.h: Ned Fritz, the father of Texas wilderness
sections.x: 1916–2008 Dallas, fighting for East Texas. Ned Fritz, the father of Texas wilderness. A Dallas lawyer who retired from his law practice in 1974 and spent the rest of his life fighting for Texas land. He founded the Texas Committee on Natural Resources, now the Texas Conservation Alliance. In 1976 he sued the Forest Service over clearcutting in our national forests, and he kept suing for decades. His endangered species case, built around the red-cockaded woodpecker, ended clearcutting on 200,000 acres of Texas national forest land and set woodpecker habitat rules across the Southeast. He also fought for the Big Thicket and helped win five wilderness areas in East Texas. Two of them, Turkey Hill and Upland Island, are in the Angelina National Forest, right here at home. Sources: Forest History Society / USDA Forest Service, history of litigation (July 2, 1976 suit); Texas Conservation Alliance (200,000 acres; woodpecker guidelines); TCA tribute (five East Texas wilderness areas); Wikipedia (retired 1974); Sierra Club Houston (Turkey Hill and Upland Island wilderness, Angelina National Forest)

1993–2005 Caddo Lake, Harrison County. Dwight K. Shellman Jr. Everybody knows Don Henley helped save Caddo Lake. Fewer know the Colorado lawyer Henley recruited to do the work. Dwight Shellman came in December 1992, moved part time to the lake, and made friends with the people who lived there. Through the Caddo Lake Institute, the lake was named a Wetland of International Importance in 1993. He organized the first real scientific study of the lake, and pushed for years to turn a closed Army ammunition plant on the south shore into a wildlife refuge. When Caddo Lake National Wildlife Refuge finally opened in September 2009, he was too sick with ALS to attend. The visitor center there carries his name. Sources: Associated Press via Pollstar, May 3, 2011 (recruitment, research, refuge, 2009 opening); Caddo Lake Institute (visitor center named for him; president 1993–2005); Wikipedia, “Caddo Lake” (Ramsar designation, Oct. 23, 1993)

sections.h: The folks who kept the Neches running
sections.x: 2006–2010 The upper Neches River. The folks who kept the Neches running. For decades the state had the upper Neches marked for a Dallas reservoir called Lake Fastrill. In 2006 the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service approved a 25,281-acre wildlife refuge in the same footprint instead. Dallas and the Texas Water Development Board sued. East Texans fought back, led by the Texas Conservation Alliance under Janice Bezanson and the Friends of the Neches River. They argued Dallas could get its water from reservoirs it already had. In February 2010 the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear the case, and the refuge stood. Sound familiar? A big city wanted East Texas water, and the state’s water agency was on its side. Neighbors who did their homework won anyway. Sources: Pacific Standard (25,281-acre refuge approved June 2006); National Wildlife Federation, June/July 2010 (Dallas and TWDB suit; Supreme Court declined; TCA led the fight); Big Thicket Reporter #104 (Bezanson and Michael Banks of Friends of the Neches River, Feb. 22, 2010); Texas Observer (existing reservoirs argument)

From our own county’s history. The 1976 county history and Winnie Graham’s memoir are full of people who stood their ground. Here are a few. There’s more on Land of the Little Angel , Black heritage and Under the black gum tree

Born 1833 Lufkin. George Hackney. Born into slavery in Tennessee, sold at the New Orleans slave market, and brought to the Angelina River plantation of James Ewing, where he worked as a blacksmith and teamster. Freedom came on June 19, 1865. The county history says Ewing told him he could go, and threatened to kill him if he stopped within a hundred miles. He settled in Lufkin anyway. He bought land and town lots, ran a boarding house, and met the night trains to see travelers safely to their beds, at a time when the county history says few Black men could be seen in town after dark. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin, 1976), pp. 274–275

About 1900 Pollok. Henry Claybon. When a sawmill company came for his land at Pollok, he wouldn’t sell. He leased it instead, for 200 pounds of salt pork and four barrels of flour a year, for as long as the mill ran or 99 years. A landowner who kept his land on his own terms. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin, 1976), p. 162

1857 Jonesville. Chief Justice Joseph Herrington. When commissioners tried to move the county seat without following the law, he said no. A man who wasn’t a sworn commissioner had acted, and only three commissioners had done business when four were required. He declared their acts void. The county’s oldest lesson in process: if they skip the rules, it doesn’t count. He’d been there from the start. When the county was organized in 1846, the Legislature named him one of six men to set its lines and choose Marion as the first seat, and at 22 he was elected the county’s first chief justice. He served five terms and is buried in the Herrington family cemetery near Huntington, where a state historical marker stands. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin, 1976), p. 23; Texas Historical Commission marker 7003 (1982)

1970s Angelina County. Rep. John Hannah. One of the reform-minded “Dirty Thirty” legislators in the Sharpstown scandal years, he later served as district attorney and then lobbied for Common Cause Texas, a government-accountability group. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin, 1976), pp. 35–37, 217

sections.h: Olivia Hackney and Coach Elmer Redd
sections.x: 1931–1969 Lufkin. Olivia Hackney and Coach Elmer Redd. Olivia Ray Hackney taught at Dunbar School from 1931; in 1964 Carver School was renamed Hackney in her honor. Coach Elmer Redd built Dunbar into one of the great programs in Texas: three state football titles and a 143–35 record. They built something excellent with less, and the community still remembers. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin, 1976), pp. 49–51, 200–202, 245

1928 Texas Forest Service. Knox Ivie, the smoke chaser. Hired at $85 a month to watch the woods for fire from a crow’s nest in a tall hickory. He raised a 78-foot pole lookout and built a tree cab that was struck by lightning hours after he finished it. Before the towers, men like him kept the cutover woods from burning while they grew back. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin, 1976), pp. 189–190

1922–2004 Zavalla. Cmdr. Arthur Ray Hawkins. A Zavalla boy taught to fly by Lufkin’s A. O. McQueen. He became one of the Navy’s top aces of World War II, with 14 aerial victories and three Navy Crosses, and later led the Blue Angels. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin, 1976), pp. 141–142; National Aviation Hall of Fame

Fighting right now. Not every steward is history. These East Texas fights are still going, and the people in them are writing the next chapter. Some of these cases are still in court, so we stick to what’s on the record. 2025–now Anderson, Henderson and Houston counties. The rural uprising over the Carrizo-Wilcox. Companies tied to Dallas investor Kyle Bass applied to pump roughly 15 billion gallons a year out of the Carrizo-Wilcox through dozens of high-capacity wells, to export it out of the area. Neighbors packed the Neches & Trinity Valleys Groundwater Conservation District meeting in Jacksonville in June 2025. Wayne-Sanderson Farms, which contracts with hundreds of family farms, sued the district. The fight reached an 11-hour legislative committee hearing, and the district voided the original permits in a settlement. A judge later issued a final judgment and permanent injunction pausing the project until studies are done. On May 21, 2026, the district adopted a moratorium on new permits for projects that don’t serve local use. The Bass companies sued in federal court in Tyler that July, and in October 2026 one piece of the fight was argued before the 12th Court of Appeals. Sources: Grist (about 15 billion gallons; June 19 Jacksonville meeting); KLTV, July 21, 2025 (Sanderson lawsuit; family farms; three counties); Texas Tribune, Oct. 21, 2025 (11-hour hearing; permits voided); Tyler Morning Telegraph, Nov. 27, 2025 (final judgment and permanent injunction); Texas Tribune, July 8, 2026 (May 21, 2026 moratorium; federal suit); Texas Lawbook (12th Court of Appeals arguments). 2025–now Lake O’ the Pines. David Simpson and Lake O’ the Pines. East Texans have opposed a proposed sale of Lake O’ the Pines water to the Dallas-area North Texas Municipal Water District since the news broke in January 2025. Former state Rep. David Simpson of Avinger sued the water district that manages the lake, saying it broke the Texas Open Meetings Act by negotiating the sale without public notice. Source: Tyler Morning Telegraph, Oct. 14, 2025. Know a steward we missed? A teacher who planted trees with every class, a rancher who kept his creek clean, somebody who stood up at a meeting when nobody else would. Tell us who they are and what they did, and send a source if there is one: a news story, an obituary, a plaque. Email contact@grailsystems.io. We check every name before it goes up

East Texas Legacy Coalition. What’s cooking in the Piney Woods. Food that comes out of these woods, creeks and gardens, the way it’s been made here for generations. Our members’ family recipes are coming next, starting with our founder’s

Mayhaw jelly. Mayhaws ripening on the branch. If there’s one taste that belongs to Deep East Texas, it’s this one. Mayhaws are small, tart, apple-like fruit from a thorny hawthorn that grows in wet bottomland along our creeks and rivers. In Texas they only grow north and east of the Trinity River. They bloom white in late winter and drop ripe fruit in spring, often right into the water, where folks scoop them up with sieves. J F M A M J J A S O N D. Light pink: blooming. Red: picking season. Right here in Huntington, Wynn and Pam Havard’s Jellytree Mayhaw Farm makes it the old way: mayhaws, sugar and pectin, cooked in small batches. Pam’s advice is to freeze the berries until you’re ready. She thinks jelly from frozen mayhaws turns out better. To make it safely, use a tested canning recipe. The National Center for Home Food Preservation publishes one for mayhaw jelly with pectin, with exact ratios and processing times. Canning is one place where you follow the tested recipe to the letter. Mayhaw jelly and biscuits. Get the tested mayhaw jelly recipe

From our founder’s kitchen. I learned to make mayhaw jelly with my grandmother, Pat Griffin. I called her Mamie. It was the absolute best. Mornings in her kitchen started with fresh sweet tea in her white glass pitcher with the little blue flowers on it. She’d cover it with a kitchen towel while it was still steaming hot, and we’d drink on it all day before making a new batch for supper. She and her mother, my great-grandmother Audrey Faye Jones, my Granny, were the finest two cooks in all of East Texas. Homemade spaghetti. Corned beef we cured ourselves, from our own cows. The best steak you ever ate. Somebody else owns that house now, and I often wonder if they know the legacy of the women whose kitchen they’re standing in. Fawn Elizabeth Zion, founder. Sources: Texas A&M AgriLife, “Mayhaw” (wet floodplain soils; ripens late April and early May in East Texas); Texas Highways (north and east of the Trinity; February bloom; Jellytree farm, Huntington); Texas Highways, “Mayhaw jelly” (sieves, small batches, freezing tip); Wikipedia, “Mayhaw” (links the NCHFP tested recipe). From Mamie’s kitchen. Recipes from our founder’s grandmother, Pat Griffin, as her granddaughter remembers them. Mamie cooked by eye, so where she didn’t measure, neither do we. We added starting amounts for folks who never got to watch her

Mamie’s homemade spaghetti. Pat Griffin’s recipe. Man oh man, it was so good. Still is. You’ll need. A couple pounds of ground beef. Green bell pepper, minced. Yellow onion, minced. A couple cloves of garlic, minced. Lots of garlic powder. Italian seasoning. Oregano. Bay leaf. Parsley. Salt and pepper. Petite diced tomatoes. Tomato paste. Tomato sauce, if it needs it. A little sugar. Spaghetti noodles. How Mamie did it. Fry the ground beef, bell pepper, onion and garlic all together in a big pot. While it cooks, season it: lots of garlic powder, plus Italian seasoning, oregano, a bay leaf, parsley, salt and pepper. Add the petite diced tomatoes and tomato paste. If it needs it, add a little tomato sauce. Stir in some sugar. Let it simmer while you boil the noodles. Pull the bay leaf before serving. Starting amounts if you never watched her (our suggestion, not Mamie’s): 2 pounds beef, 1 bell pepper, 1 onion, 2 or 3 cloves garlic, 2 teaspoons garlic powder and up, 1 tablespoon Italian seasoning, 1 teaspoon oregano, 1 bay leaf, 2 cans (14.5 ounces) petite diced tomatoes, 1 can (6 ounces) tomato paste, about 1 tablespoon sugar, 1 pound spaghetti. Simmer at least 30 minutes

Garlic Texas toast. Goes with Mamie’s spaghetti. You’ll need. A loaf of Sunbeam Texas-size bread. Butter. Garlic salt. How to. Spread butter on the slices. Sprinkle with garlic salt. Bake a few minutes, until it’s golden. Our suggestion if you need a number: 400°F for 5 to 8 minutes. Watch it close

Mamie’s sweet tea. Pat Griffin’s recipe. Lipton, brewed the old-fashioned way, 6 to 8 glasses at a time. You either got it or you don’t. You’ll need. Lipton tea bags. Water. A quarter to a half cup of sugar. Ice. A glass pitcher and a kitchen towel. How Mamie did it. Brew the tea hot, the old-fashioned way. Pour in the sugar while it’s hot, a quarter to a half cup. Pour it into the pitcher and cover it with a kitchen towel while it’s still steaming. Serve it hot, poured over ice. Never saved for later. Whatever’s left goes down the sink, and you make a fresh batch for supper. Starting amounts if you never watched her (our suggestion, not Mamie’s): about 6 regular Lipton bags steeped 5 minutes in a quart of just-boiled water, then topped up to a 2-quart pitcher

Cast-iron skillet cornbread. One 10-inch skillet, about 8 wedges. The bread that goes under, beside or into most of what’s on this page. Get the skillet screaming hot first. That’s where the crust comes from. You’ll need. 2 tablespoons bacon grease or butter. 1½ cups yellow cornmeal. ½ cup all-purpose flour. 1 tablespoon baking powder. ½ teaspoon baking soda. 1 teaspoon salt. 1½ cups buttermilk. 2 eggs. ¼ cup melted butter. How to. Put the grease in a 10-inch cast-iron skillet and set it in the oven while it heats to 450°F. Whisk the cornmeal, flour, baking powder, baking soda and salt in a bowl. In another bowl, whisk the buttermilk, eggs and melted butter. Stir into the dry mix just until it comes together. Pull the hot skillet out, swirl the grease up the sides, and pour in the batter. It should sizzle. Bake 20 to 25 minutes, until the top is golden and a toothpick comes out clean. Turn it out onto a board and cut into wedges. Sugar or no sugar is a family argument we’re staying out of. Add up to 2 tablespoons to the dry mix if that’s how your grandmother did it

Cornmeal-fried catfish. Serves 4. Friday-night fish fry food. Cornmeal, not flour, and hot oil, not warm oil. You’ll need. 2 pounds catfish fillets, cut into strips. 1 cup buttermilk. 1 cup fine yellow cornmeal. ¼ cup all-purpose flour. 2 teaspoons salt. 1 teaspoon black pepper. 1 teaspoon paprika. ½ teaspoon cayenne. Peanut or vegetable oil for frying. Lemon wedges and hot sauce. How to. Soak the catfish in buttermilk for 20 minutes while you heat 2 inches of oil to 350°F in a heavy pot or Dutch oven. Mix the cornmeal, flour, salt, pepper, paprika and cayenne in a shallow dish. Lift each strip from the buttermilk, let it drip, and press it into the cornmeal mix on both sides. Fry a few pieces at a time, 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and the fish flakes. Fish is done at 145°F inside. Drain on a rack. Salt again while hot. Serve with lemon, hot sauce and hushpuppies. Don’t crowd the pot. Too many pieces at once drops the oil temperature and you get greasy fish

Hushpuppies. About 2 dozen. Fry these in the same oil right after the catfish. You’ll need. 1 cup yellow cornmeal. ½ cup all-purpose flour. 2 teaspoons baking powder. 1 teaspoon salt. 1 tablespoon sugar. ½ cup finely chopped onion. 1 jalapeño, seeded and minced (optional). 1 egg. ¾ cup buttermilk. How to. Stir together the cornmeal, flour, baking powder, salt and sugar. Stir in the onion and jalapeño, then the egg and buttermilk. The batter should be thick enough to hold a shape on a spoon. With oil at 350°F, drop tablespoon-size scoops in and fry 2 to 3 minutes, turning, until brown all over. Drain and eat them hot

Chicken and rolled dumplings. Serves 6. Flat, rolled dumplings, the kind you cut with a knife. Sunday dinner, sick-day dinner, and what shows up on the porch when somebody passes. You’ll need. 1 whole chicken (about 4 pounds). 1 onion, quartered. 2 ribs celery. 2 teaspoons salt, plus more to taste. 1 teaspoon black pepper. For the dumplings: 2 cups all-purpose flour. ½ teaspoon baking powder. ½ teaspoon salt. 3 tablespoons cold butter or shortening. ¾ cup cold milk or broth. How to. Cover the chicken with water in a big pot with the onion, celery, salt and pepper. Simmer about 1 hour, until the meat falls off the bone. Take out the chicken. Strain the broth and put it back on to simmer. Pull the meat off the bones in bite-size pieces. For the dumplings, mix the flour, baking powder and salt. Cut in the butter until it looks like coarse crumbs. Stir in the milk to make a stiff dough. Roll the dough thin, about ⅛ inch, on a floured counter. Cut into strips about 1 by 2 inches. Drop the strips one at a time into the simmering broth. Cover and cook 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Stir the chicken back in and cook 5 minutes more. The broth will thicken from the flour. Taste for salt and pepper. Chicken is safe at 165°F

Hot wassail. About 12 cups. Every Saturday after Thanksgiving, downtown Nacogdoches merchants brew their best wassail and let shoppers vote for a winner. This is a simple version to make at home. There’s no alcohol in it. You’ll need. 2 quarts apple cider. 2 cups orange juice. 1 cup pineapple juice. ½ cup lemon juice. ½ cup sugar or honey, to taste. 3 cinnamon sticks. 1 teaspoon whole cloves. 1 teaspoon whole allspice. 1 orange, sliced. How to. Put everything in a big pot or slow cooker. Bring to a bare simmer, then turn the heat to low. Don’t let it boil hard. Keep it warm for at least 30 minutes so the spices steep. Strain out the whole spices before serving, or ladle around them. Source for the tradition: Visit Nacogdoches, Wassail Fest and Country Roads Magazine

sections.h: Put your family’s recipe on the table
sections.x: Put your family’s recipe on the table. Got a recipe that came down from somebody? Ribbon cane syrup, a sweet potato pie, the way your granddaddy did squirrel, a church cookbook page with grease stains on it? Send it to contact@grailsystems.io with who it came from, what part of East Texas, and a photo if you have one. We’ll credit your family by name, or leave it anonymous if you’d rather

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: East Texas Legacy Coalition. NPS photo by Scott Sharaga, Big Thicket National Preserve What grows wild in the Piney Woods. The mayhaw slough down by the creek, the persimmon on the fence row, the chanterelles after a summer rain. These are the wild foods of Deep East Texas, and the plants and mushrooms that can hurt you if you mistake them for one. Read this first. This page is for learning and for honoring what our people knew. It is not a field guide. Never eat a wild plant or mushroom because a website says it’s safe, this one included. Have someone who knows confirm it in person, every time. Many edible plants and mushrooms have poisonous look-alikes, and some of those can kill. If someone eats something and you’re not sure what it was, call the Texas Poison Center Network right away, any hour of any day. Don’t wait for symptoms; with some mushrooms they take hours to show. In an emergency, call 911. 1-800-222-1222

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: The year in the woods. When each one is ready, as far as our sources say. Where a source gives a season but not months, we wrote it out instead of guessing. J F M A M J J A S O N D Mayhaw Dewberry Pawpaw Elderberry Muscadine Chickasaw plum Persimmon After the first frost, once the leaves have fallen Farkleberry Ripens in fall, and the berries hang on through winter Chanterelle Spring through early fall, when it’s been wet Chicken of the woods Often in fall, on oaks. Blooming Ready to pick

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Ask before you pick. Our grandparents picked where they had permission to pick, and the rules still matter. Private land: get the owner’s OK first. Texas state parks: picking or removing any plant life without a permit from the director is an offense under state park rules. Big Thicket National Preserve: you may gather a reasonable amount for personal use from a set list: pawpaw, mayhaw, wild grape, wild strawberry, wild blueberry, wild huckleberry, blackberry, dewberry, mulberry, walnut, pecan and hickory nuts. Carry no more than a one-quart container home, and sell none of it. Mushrooms are not on the list. Angelina, Davy Crockett, Sabine and Sam Houston National Forests: check with the ranger district before you gather anything. Sources: 31 Tex. Admin. Code §59.134(l)(1) ; Big Thicket National Preserve, Superintendent’s Compendium (revised June 2026), 36 CFR 2.1(c)

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Mayhaw. Crataegus species, a hawthorn. The taste of Deep East Texas. Small, tart, apple-like fruit from a thorny hawthorn that grows in wet bottomland along our creeks and rivers. In Texas, mayhaws grow only north and east of the Trinity River. They bloom white in February and drop ripe fruit in late April and early May, often right into the water. How we eat it: jelly, made with a tested canning recipe. The story and the recipe are on our recipes page. Sources: Texas A&M AgriLife, “Mayhaw” ; Texas Highways

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Dewberry and blackberry. Rubus species. Dewberries are wild blackberries on a low, trailing vine. Southern dewberry grows from East through Central Texas along roadsides, fence rows and thickets, and bears heavily in spring and early summer. Jesse Truvillion remembered picking blackberries in the Big Thicket for pie, and for wine for the Lord’s Supper. How we eat it: fresh, in cobbler, pie and jam. Sources: KPRC Click2Houston (range, habitat, season); National Park Service, “Relying on the Landscape”

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Muscadine. Vitis rotundifolia. Our native grape. Muscadines grow wild from the eastern third of Texas, where the soil is acidic and rain is heavy, east to Maryland. They hang in small clusters of big berries that ripen one at a time and drop when they’re ready. Wild vines are male or female, so only some bear fruit. When: most muscadines ripen from mid-August through September in East Texas. How we eat it: fresh, or as jelly, jam and wine. The seeds are hard and often bitter. Muscadine. Several small, round seeds. Curling tendrils. Toothed leaves. Common moonseed. Poisonous. Blue-black berries in grape-like clusters, ripe about the same time. One flat, crescent-moon seed. No tendrils; leaves not toothed. Sources: Texas A&M AgriLife, “Muscadine cultivars” ; AgriLife, “Muscadine” (ripening); Missouri Dept. of Conservation, “Common Moonseed” ; NC State Extension ; Wikipedia (range west to Texas)

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: American persimmon. Diospyros virginiana. The “possum apple.” American persimmon grows wild across the South and west into Texas as far as the Colorado River, often in groves along fence rows and old pastures. Its range takes in the Caddo homeland too. When: usually after the first frost, once the leaves have fallen. How we eat it: only when soft and fully ripe. An unripe persimmon is so astringent it will pucker your whole mouth, and even after frost some fruit stays that way. American persimmon fruit on the tree. Photo: Steven J. Baskauf, Bioimages , CC BY 4.0. Sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, “Persimmons” (E-611); Texas Beyond History (Caddo homeland); Wikipedia (“possum apple”)

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Pawpaw. Asimina triloba. The largest edible fruit native to the United States. Pawpaw grows in thickets along stream banks and in rich, damp bottomland woods, and its range reaches south into eastern Texas. When: blooms April to May; the fruit ripens later in the year. Take care: handling the fruit can irritate skin, and some people get bad stomach and intestinal pain from eating it. Try a little first. Pawpaw fruit. Photo: Steven J. Baskauf, Bioimages , CC BY 4.0. Sources: USDA Forest Service, Fire Effects Information System (range); Native Plant Society of Texas, “Pawpaw” ; Wikipedia, “Asimina” (largest native fruit)

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: American beautyberry. Callicarpa americana. A native shrub of the Southeast with bright purple berry clusters. The berries are edible, but raw they’re mealy and bland. Cooked into jelly, they’re a different story. Delena Tull’s Edible and Useful Plants of Texas and the Southwest says the later in the season you pick them, the better. How we eat it: jelly. Sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center, “Mr. Smarty Plants” (quoting Tull); Missouri Dept. of Conservation ; Florida Wildflower Foundation. Beautyberry in the native plant beds at The History Center in Diboll. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Elderberry. Sambucus nigra ssp. canadensis. A shrub of wet ground along fence rows, streams and low places in East Texas, with flat clusters of white flowers and then dark berries. How we eat it: the ripe berries, always cooked. The leaves, stems and roots are poisonous, and raw or unripe berries can make you sick. Pick off every stem. Elderberry. A woody shrub with white flower clusters, then dark berries. Spotted water hemlock. Deadly. Same wet ground, often right beside elderberry, with the same kind of white flower clusters. Smooth, hollow, soft stems, often streaked purple. More below. Elderberries on the bush. Photo: Steven J. Baskauf, Bioimages , CC BY 4.0. Sources: USGS, “Sambucus nigra” ; Native Plant Society of Texas (bloom); Oregon State Extension (always cook); Missouri Dept. of Conservation ; Florida Wildflower Foundation (grows alongside elderberry); UF/IFAS Extension (woody vs. smooth stems); UF/IFAS, Duval County (hollow, purple-streaked stems)

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Wild plums. Prunus species, including Chickasaw plum (P. angustifolia). Winnie Graham wrote that her grandfather could walk straight to the wild plums in the Oak Flat woods without a trail. Chickasaw plum, one of the native wild plums of Texas, grows into thorny thickets with fragrant white flowers in spring. Some trees bear good fruit and some bear very bitter fruit, so not every tree is worth the picking. When: Chickasaw plums fruit from June into August. How we eat it: fresh, or as jam and jelly. Its fruit has long been made into wine, jam and jelly. Chickasaw plum in bloom. Photo: Steven J. Baskauf, Bioimages , CC BY 4.0. Sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide, Chickasaw plum ; USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet ; Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree (2013), pp. 9–11, 70–75

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Farkleberry. Vaccinium arboreum. A wild blueberry that grows into a small tree, also called sparkleberry, tree huckleberry and winter huckleberry. In 1976 the national champion farkleberry stood near Zavalla, 29 feet tall, in the creek country of Sandy, Turpentine, Shawnee and Possum Walk creeks. You can see one at the Pineywoods Native Plant Center in Nacogdoches. When: the shiny black berries ripen in fall and hang on through winter. How we eat it: fresh. They're edible and sweet, but dry and mealy, and some bushes taste better than others. Farkleberry fruit, up close. Photo: Steven J. Baskauf, Bioimages , CC BY 4.0. Sources: Missouri Dept. of Conservation ; UF/IFAS (ripening); Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center (Pineywoods Native Plant Center); Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel (1976), p. 221

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Yaupon. Ilex vomitoria. The evergreen holly that grows all through the East Texas woods. It's the only plant native to North America with caffeine in it, and Native peoples across the Southeast brewed its leaves. Despite the name, a tea of the leaves can be safely drunk. At Oak Flat, country folks hung a sprig of it, red berries and all, for Christmas. How we use it: dried leaves, brewed as tea. Take care: the red berries are toxic to people. Birds can eat them; you can't. Yaupon leaves, the part that’s brewed. Photo: Steven J. Baskauf, Bioimages , CC BY 4.0. Sources: Texas Master Naturalists, Lost Pines (East Texas range; only native caffeinated plant); Texas Master Naturalists, Coastal Prairie (tea safe; berries toxic); NPR ; Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree , p. 137

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Sassafras and filé. Sassafras albidum. A native tree of the eastern United States. Its dried, ground young leaves are filé powder, the seasoning and thickener stirred into gumbo after it comes off the heat. How we use it: leaves, dried and ground into filé. Take care: the old root-bark tea is a different story. Sassafras root bark and oil are high in safrole, which the FDA has banned as a food additive over cancer concerns. Skip the root tea. Sassafras leaves, the part that’s dried for filé. Photo: Steven J. Baskauf, Bioimages , CC BY 4.0. Sources: Wikipedia, “Filé powder” ; Memorial Sloan Kettering, “Sassafras” ; Drugs.com (safrole in root bark)

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Pecan, hickory and walnut. Carya and Juglans species. Pecans are native from Indiana and Illinois south to Louisiana and Texas. Hickory nuts were a common thing to gather in the Big Thicket, and pecan, hickory and walnut are all on the preserve’s list of foods you may gather for personal use. Black walnuts still in their green husks. Photo: Steven J. Baskauf, Bioimages , CC BY 4.0. Sources: National Wildlife Federation (pecan range); National Park Service, “Relying on the Landscape” ; Big Thicket Compendium. Della Burchfield and Gertrude Waltman White picking berries along the railroad near Fastrill, 1935. A hand-tinted print. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Leave these alone. These grow in our part of Texas. Learn them before you learn anything else

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Spotted water hemlock. Cicuta maculata. Deadly. The most toxic plant in North America, and every part of it is deadly. A piece of root the size of a walnut can kill an animal the size of a cow. In Texas it grows in the east, center and north of the state, always near water: streams, marshes, wet meadows and springs. It has white umbrella-shaped flower clusters and smooth, hollow stems often streaked purple, and it can be mistaken for wild carrot (Queen Anne’s lace) and elderberry. Sources: Texas A&M, Toxic Plants of Texas ; Missouri Dept. of Conservation ; USGS (wild carrot confusion); UF/IFAS, Duval County

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Pokeweed. Phytolacca americana. Poisonous. Tall, with reddish-purple stems and drooping clusters of dark purple berries. It grows in the eastern two-thirds of Texas, often in disturbed sandy ground and old brush piles. The berries and roots are poisonous to people. People have long eaten “poke sallet,” young leaves boiled with the water changed to carry off the toxins, but Mississippi State Extension considers every part of the plant toxic. We don’t recommend it. Sources: Texas A&M, “Pokeberry, Pokeweed” ; Texas A&M, Toxic Plants of Texas (archived) ; Native Plant Society of Texas ; Mississippi State Extension, “Forgotten Foods”

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Jimsonweed. Datura species. Poisonous, every part. A coarse, bad-smelling weed with big white to purple trumpet flowers and a spiny seed pod. Several kinds grow in Texas, including the Pineywoods. The leaves and seeds carry the most poison, the same drugs as atropine and scopolamine. In 1676 soldiers at Jamestown ate it boiled as greens, and it's been called Jamestown weed ever since. Don't confuse it with angel's trumpet, which is just as dangerous: jimsonweed flowers point up, angel's trumpet flowers hang down. Jimsonweed in flower. Every part is poisonous. Photo: Steven J. Baskauf, Bioimages , CC BY 4.0. Sources: Texas A&M, Toxic Plants of Texas ; Texas A&M, Toxic Plants of Texas (archived; Pineywoods) ; NC State Extension (flowers up vs. down); Cornell (Jamestown); MedlinePlus

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Carolina jessamine. Gelsemium sempervirens. Poisonous, every part. The yellow trumpet-flowered vine that lights up our woods and fence rows in late winter and early spring, the "yellow jasmine" Winnie Graham remembered in March. Every part carries toxins related to strychnine. Children have been poisoned by sucking the nectar from the flowers, so teach yours to leave it be. Sources: USGS ; UF/IFAS ; Clemson Extension (nectar); Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center ; Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree , pp. 9–11

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Strawberry bush. Euonymus americanus. Poisonous. Not a strawberry. Also called hearts-a-bustin'. In fall its warty pink-red pods look a little like strawberries, then split open on bright orange-red seeds. The fruit, seeds and bark are poisonous, and the seeds are a harsh laxative. Winnie Graham wondered if it was the "strawberry" of an old song; it's a pretty plant, but not one to eat. Sources: Florida Museum of Natural History ; Wikipedia (laxative seeds); Winnie Graham, Under the Blackgum Tree , p. 145

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Mayapple. Podophyllum peltatum. Poisonous, except one part, and only just. Umbrella-shaped leaves in colonies on the forest floor. Every part is poisonous except the fully ripe, soft, yellow fruit, and even that is safe only in small amounts. The green fruit, leaves and roots are toxic. It's also called wild mandrake, but it isn't the mandrake of old stories. Mayapple in flower. Photo: Steven J. Baskauf, Bioimages , CC BY 4.0. Sources: NC State Extension ; Missouri Dept. of Conservation ; Winnie Graham, Listening to Plants (2020), p. 51

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Taking over our woods. Some plants here don't belong here, and they crowd out the mayhaws, berries and nut trees our people gathered. Texas A&M Forest Service lists 12 common invasive plants in the East Texas landscape. If you're clearing land or planting a yard, learn these and don't plant them. Chinese tallow Brought from China in the 1700s for its waxy seeds and as an ornamental. A tree up to 60 feet that seeds heavily and crowds out native plants. Kudzu The vine that ate the South, brought from Asia for erosion control. It smothers whole trees. Japanese climbing fern Brought in as an ornamental in the 1930s. A twining fern that mats over open forest, road edges and wet places. And nine more Chinese privet, Japanese honeysuckle, Asian bamboos, chinaberry, Chinese wisteria, giant reed, mimosa, tropical soda apple and giant Asian dodder. Sources: Texas A&M Forest Service, “Common Invasive Plants in East Texas” ; TFS fact sheet ; TFS, “Invasive, non-native and native species explained”. Winnie Graham wrote about kudzu in Listening to Plants , pp. 67–68

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Mushrooms. East Texas has the heaviest rainfall in the state and forests of pine, oak and beech. Mycologist David Lewis calls it “the last frontier” for mushroom hunters; he has found 550 species on his own 60 acres. Don’t eat any wild mushroom because of this page or any website. Take it, whole, to a local expert first. Every edible below has a look-alike that can make you very sick, and some white mushrooms in our woods can kill you. Source: Texas Observer, “Fungi Town”

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Chanterelles. Cantharellus species. Golden, orange and cinnabar-red chanterelles grow on the ground in our oak and pine woods. Mycologists have collected them in the Big Thicket’s Big Sandy Creek, Turkey Creek and Lance Rosier units. Texas has 15 or more kinds. When: spring through early fall, when it’s been wet. What to look for: they grow from soil, not wood. Underneath, instead of true, sharp gills they have blunt, shallow ridges, or a nearly smooth surface. Chanterelle. Grows from soil. Blunt ridges or a smooth underside. Jack-o’-lantern. Poisonous, bright orange. Dense clusters on stumps, dead trees or buried roots, so it can look like it’s coming from the ground. True, sharp-edged gills. Severe cramps, vomiting and diarrhea that can last for days. Have an expert confirm every chanterelle in person before you eat it. Sources: Encyclopedia of Life (Big Sandy Creek Unit); New York Botanical Garden herbarium (Turkey Creek Unit); Thicket of Diversity (Lance Rosier Unit); Texas Highways (season; 15+ species); UF/IFAS (look-alikes); Missouri Dept. of Conservation ; Central Texas Mycological Society (southern jack-o’-lantern); Univ. of Virginia, Mountain Lake Biological Station (symptoms)

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Chicken of the woods. Laetiporus species. Big overlapping shelves, orange on top and sulfur-yellow underneath, growing out of oak trees and logs, often in fall. What to look for: the underside has tiny pores, not gills. Take care: raw or undercooked, it has made people sick, and some people are allergic to it even cooked. Cook it well and try only a little the first time. Chicken of the woods. Shelves on wood. Pores underneath. Jack-o’-lantern. Also bright orange, also on wood. Gills underneath. Have an expert confirm it in person before you eat it. Sources: Missouri Dept. of Conservation ; Central Texas Mycological Society (oaks, fall, in Texas); UF/IFAS, “Chicken of the Woods” (raw, allergy); Missouri Conservationist (jack-o’-lantern gills)

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Puffballs. Calvatia and Lycoperdon species. Round white mushrooms with no cap and no stem, from small ones to the huge giant puffball. As they age, the inside turns yellow-green and then to dusty spores. The one rule: cut every single one in half, top to bottom. An edible puffball is solid, pure white and spongy all the way through, with nothing inside it. Throw it out if: you see any shape inside, like the outline of a cap and gills; or it's yellow, green, brown, purple or black inside. Yellowing means it's too old and can make you sick. Puffball. Cut in half: solid white , no structure at all. Destroying angel "egg". Deadly. A young Amanita can look just like a small puffball from outside. Cut in half, it shows the outline of a mushroom : cap, gills and stem. Earthballs, also poisonous, are dark inside. Have an expert confirm it in person before you eat it. Sources: Missouri Dept. of Conservation, “Giant Puffball” (white interior; destroying angel look-alike); Thomas J. Duffy, MD, Toxic Fungi of Western North America (Amanita button cut in half; discolored interior); Forager Chef (earthballs dark inside)

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Destroying angel. Amanita bisporigera. Deadly. Never eat a white mushroom from the woods. One of the most poisonous mushrooms on earth, and it grows here: it has been photographed at the Watson Rare Native Plant Preserve in Warren and in the Big Thicket. It is all white, with white gills, a skirt-like ring on the stem, and a sac-like cup at the base that is often hidden underground. It carries amatoxins, the same poison as the death cap. People mistake it for button and meadow mushrooms, and young ones for puffballs. Symptoms can take hours to start, after the poison is already at work. If anyone eats a wild white mushroom, call 1-800-222-1222 right away. Sources: Texas Mushrooms (Watson Preserve and Big Thicket photos); Missouri Dept. of Conservation ; Wikipedia (amatoxins; look-alikes); Poison Control (delayed symptoms)

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: Green-spored parasol. Chlorophyllum molybdites. Poisonous, and probably in your yard. A big white mushroom with cream to brown scales that pops up in lawns and pastures across the Southeast, often in a ring. It has been reported as the most common cause of mushroom poisoning in the United States, with severe vomiting and diarrhea that usually start within one to three hours. People confuse it with edible parasol and shaggy mane mushrooms. As it ages, its gills turn grayish-green, and it leaves a green spore print. Keep children and pets away from lawn mushrooms. Sources: UF/IFAS, “The Green-Spore Poison Parasol Mushroom” (citing Lehmann 1992); Missouri Dept. of Conservation ; Wikipedia (look-alikes, onset)

sections.t: Wild foods of Deep East Texas
sections.x: From our family bookshelf. Our founder’s aunt, Winnie Graham, wrote down what the Piney Woods taught her family. A sixth-generation Texan with deep family roots in these woods, she earned a degree in electrical engineering from Louisiana State University and studied anthropology at UCLA. Under the Blackgum Tree: 165 Years in the Piney Woods. Stephen F. Austin State University Press, 2013. 200 pages. She set out to write down a few family tales for the younger generation, but, as she put it, “the Piney Woods kept butting in.” The memoir is built around her family’s stories, with the lore and way of life of the Piney Woods, back to the earliest settlers, given their share. Listening to Plants: A Pathway to New Uses. Independently published, 2020. 83 pages. A book about our partnership with the plant kingdom: how people found new uses for plants over the centuries, from chewing gum to modern medicines. We’ve read both books for the wild foods her family knew. The family’s mayhaw skiffs, muscadine jelly, bitterweed milk, sweet gum “chewing gum” and Grandma Wade’s oak-gall ink are on Piney Woods ways , and the family itself is on Under the black gum tree. Anything we bring onto this page from them is checked against today’s science first and credited to her with the page number. Sources: Amazon, “Under the Blackgum Tree” (publisher, date, pages, author biography, description); Amazon, “Listening to Plants” (publisher, date, pages); Goodreads (description)

East Texas Legacy Coalition. Power and land Who decides the route? Every big change in this county started with a few people deciding where something would go: a railroad, a town, a mill, a highway. Here’s how those calls got made, from the county’s own history

1882 The railroad picks the town. Lufkin wasn’t settled and then reached by the railroad. The railroad came first. The Houston, East & West Texas line reached Denman Springs in October 1882, and town lots were sold that September on credit at 8% interest. Within ten years, people were pushing to move the county seat from Homer to the new rail town. The county history notes that one argument was getting the land records close to the railroad, where land agents could get at them easily. Lufkin became the county seat in 1892. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976)

1900 A town sold at auction. Huntington began the same way. Two promoters, E. A. Blount of Nacogdoches and W. J. Townsend of Lufkin, filed a plat in June 1900 and auctioned the lots on June 22 to the highest bidders. They named the town for C. P. Huntington, who ran the Southern Pacific. The rail line, not the people, set the spot. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976)

sections.h: The mill, the money and the newspaper
sections.x: 1934–1940 The mill, the money and the newspaper. Southland Paper Mills, the first plant to make newsprint from Southern pine, was built east of Lufkin on what had been a cotton field. Ground was broken Jan. 14, 1939, and the first roll came off the machine Jan. 17, 1940. The county history says the backers pledged nearly 110,000 acres of timberland and half of a railroad as security, then asked a federal agency, the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, for a loan of about $3.4 million. Public credit helped build a private mill. In 1934, while the Lufkin Daily News was promoting that mill, a group led by J. H. Kurth, W. C. Trout and the Hendersons bought the paper. The people with the most to gain owned the newspaper telling the story. Plain words. What all these words mean. Aquifer. Water stored underground in sand and rock, like a soaked sponge. Wells pull from it. Carrizo-Wilcox. The big aquifer under Deep East Texas. Lufkin, Nacogdoches and many family wells drink from it. Recharge. Rain soaking back into an aquifer. Here it happens slowly, mostly where the sand comes up to the surface. Brackish. Slightly salty groundwater. Fine for some industrial uses, not for drinking without treatment. Acre-foot. Enough water to cover an acre a foot deep, about 326,000 gallons. Groundwater district (GCD). The local board that permits big wells. Ours is the Pineywoods Groundwater Conservation District. Rule of capture. The old Texas rule that lets a landowner pump the water under their land, even if it drains a neighbor’s well. Districts can limit it. Public information request (PIA). A written request for government records under the Texas Public Information Act. The agency is on a legal clock to answer. P&Z. The City’s Planning and Zoning Commission. It handles zoning inside city limits. SUP. Specific use permit: City permission for a use the zoning doesn’t normally allow. ETJ. Extraterritorial jurisdiction: a band of land just outside city limits where the City has some say. The old Southland mill sits outside city limits

1853 Water ran the first mills. One of the county’s early mills ran on the water of Mill Creek. The county history names Berry Roberts, an enslaved man, as one of the people who worked it. Some of the county’s first industry ran on water power and enslaved labor. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976); see also our Mill Creek page

1840s–1877 When the Angelina carried boats. From the 1840s, steamboats and barges hauled cotton down the Angelina and Neches. The Laura ran from Brown’s Ferry in Angelina County to Sabine Pass. The county history says the river carried less water as farmland spread and the springs that fed it were plowed under, and boats got stranded in low water. River commerce faded once the railroads came. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976)

sections.h: A town born at a spring
sections.x: 1882–1891 A town born at a spring. Lufkin began at a crossroads called Denman Springs, where the railroad arrived in 1882. When the town incorporated in 1890, its legal boundary was drawn from “the head of Brushy Creek” and from Denman Spring. The springs came first; the town was drawn around them. The county history dates the first part of Lufkin’s waterworks to 1891, with a storage tank called “the standpipe” in the middle of Cotton Square, and credits Mayor T. C. Mantooth’s time with the first waterworks system. A city engineer, P. A. McCarthy, later built the sewer system. A town’s water is public business from day one. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 25, 152–153, 285, 290

sections.h: A forest to protect the watershed
sections.x: 1936 A forest to protect the watershed. The Angelina National Forest was proclaimed in October 1936. The federal law behind national forests in the East, the 1911 Weeks Act, let the government buy forest and cut-over land in the watersheds of navigable streams to protect their flow. Protecting water was part of the reason our national forests exist. Sources: 16 U.S.C. 515 (Weeks Act of March 1, 1911) ; U.S. Forest Service, National Forests and Grasslands in Texas

1949 A river authority is born. In 1949 the Legislature split the old Sabine-Neches Conservation District, creating the Neches River Conservation District. In 1977 it was renamed the Angelina & Neches River Authority. It’s still headquartered in Lufkin. Sources: Angelina & Neches River Authority, “History”

sections.h: A countywide water district, on paper
sections.x: 1957 A countywide water district, on paper. In 1957 the county commissioners created Angelina County Water Control and Improvement District No. 2, covering about 640,000 acres, more than the 514,368 acres in the whole county. A smaller WCID No. 1 was created in 1958 and later dissolved. The 1976 county history doesn’t say what No. 2 ever did. Does it still exist, and what powers does it hold? That’s a question for a records request. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976), pp. 181, 193

sections.h: Rayburn was built to store water for industry
sections.x: 1956–1966 Rayburn was built to store water for industry. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers built Sam Rayburn Reservoir from 1956 to 1966. Its stated purposes were hydroelectric power and storing water for cities and industry. The Lower Neches Valley Authority, based downstream near Beaumont, held a contract to buy water from it. So the largest lake built entirely inside Texas wasn’t built only for fishing and boating. From the start, it was a water bank, and downstream industry held an account. Sources: Bob Bowman, ed., Land of the Little Angel: A History of Angelina County, Texas (Lufkin: Lufkin Printing Co., 1976); Lower Neches Valley Authority (founded 1933)

sections.t: We’ve watched our water drop before
sections.h: Two wells that tell the story
sections.x: East Texas Legacy Coalition. We’ve watched our water drop before. For decades, the paper mill outside Lufkin was the biggest straw in Angelina County. The state measured our water dropping nearly 500 feet while it pumped, and coming back when it cut back. Now a data center wants to build on the same site. Here’s the history, straight from the state’s own reports. Two wells that tell the story. The state has measured these two wells north of Lufkin since the 1930s and ’40s. Each bar shows how far down you had to go to reach water, the first time it was measured and the latest time. Rocky Shoals on the Neches River, July 2009. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas. Depth to water in two Angelina County wells State well 3735401: about 56 feet down in 1939, 290 feet down in 2024. State well 3735701: about 190 feet down in 1946, 377 feet down in 2026. Ground level 100 ft 200 ft 300 ft 400 ft 1939: 56 ft 2024: 290 ft 1946: 190 ft 2026: 377 ft Well 3735401 down 234 ft Well 3735701 down 188 ft The light line is where the water sat the first time each well was measured. The dark line is where it sits now. The shaded gap between them is how far it has dropped. Source: Texas Water Development Board groundwater database, state well numbers 3735401 (industrial well, 76 measurements) and 3735701 (public supply well, 47 measurements), Carrizo-Wilcox aquifer. The 1939 and 1946 depths are the latest depth minus the total drop, rounded. What the state wrote down. 1940 Southland Paper Mills opens east of Lufkin. State water-level measurements start in the late 1930s, the same time Lufkin started drawing its city water from the Carrizo and the mill started running its own Carrizo wells. KTRE (opening year); TWDB Report 110 , p. 23. 1968 The mill is the biggest water user around. In Angelina County, industry pumps 15.6 million gallons a day. Every city and water system in the county combined pumps 5. The state writes: “The largest single user in the area is Southland Paper Mills.” TWDB Report 110, pp. 22–23. 1970 The state reports that pumping has pulled water levels down nearly 500 feet near the center of pumping. At the mill’s old well field, the water now sits more than 200 feet below sea level. And it warns that the Carrizo in Angelina and Nacogdoches counties can only give about 32 million gallons a day “without causing the failure of some of the present well fields and drying up portions of the aquifer.” Pumping in the two counties is already at 26.7. That leaves room for about 5 million more. TWDB Report 110, abstract (p. 1) and p. 23. Late 1970s and 1988 The paper industry northeast of Lufkin cuts back its groundwater pumping and switches partly to lake water from Lake Kurth and Striker Creek. The state records that the declines slow, and in some wells the water rises. TWDB Report 327 (Feb. 1991), pp. 23 and 26. 1991 The state names the area between Lufkin and Nacogdoches as one of the two worst drawdown areas in East Texas, with declines of “as much as 500 feet since before World War II.” It points to industrial pumping, “especially that for the paper mills northeast of Lufkin.” TWDB Report 327, abstract and p. 23. 2007 The mill shuts down. KTRE. 2009 The City of Lufkin agrees to buy the mill’s water system, including its 13 water wells. City officials say it would let Lufkin pump about five times what it could before. KTRE (13 wells); Lufkin Daily News. 2026 Amp Z plans an AI data center on the old mill site, built out to 2,100 megawatts. Its water needs are listed as “TBD.” Seven big projects in Angelina County. “But some wells are rising.”. That’s true, and the state explained why in 1991. Picture a bathtub with straws in it. Where a big straw drinks hard, the water around it dips into a funnel. Pull the straw back, and the water slowly fills back in. Of the 19 wells the state still measures in this county, 6 have dropped and 13 have risen since they were first measured. But most of the rising wells were first measured between the 1950s and 1990s, after the big pumping had already pulled the water down. Rising from the bottom of the funnel doesn’t put the water back where it was in 1939. And three of them only go back to 2021. Sources: TWDB Report 327, p. 23; current well counts from Angelina County Watch , which updates from the state database every night. What it means now. We already ran this experiment once. The biggest straw drank, the water dropped, and it took decades to start coming back. Our reading of TWDB Reports 110 and 327. Report 110 warned in 1970 that the Carrizo was close to its safe limit around Lufkin. A new big user on the same site deserves a real water number before anybody signs a contract, not “TBD.” Try the numbers yourself. What we don’t know yet. How much water Amp Z would actually use. The public was told about 500 gallons a day. Its own county application says “TBD.”. Whether Amp Z would buy water from the City’s wells, including the old mill wells, or get it some other way. It has filed no well permits with the groundwater district. Whether the 1970 safe-yield estimate still holds today. The state has done newer groundwater studies since then, and we haven’t compared them yet. What you can do. Share this with somebody who says the water will be fine. Then ask the Lufkin City Council one question at the next meeting: how many gallons a day will the data center use, in writing? Here’s how to sign up to speak

sections.t: Leave the good water for the people
sections.h: Not all water has to be drinking water
sections.x: East Texas Legacy Coalition. Leave the good water for the people. We’re not asking anybody to shut the lights off. We’re asking that the water we drink go to people, and that servers get cooled with other water. Lufkin already owns some. It bought it for industry in 2009. Not all water has to be drinking water. A cooling tower doesn’t need water clean enough to drink. Here are the kinds of water around Lufkin, and what each one is good for. October morning mist on the Neches River. Courtesy of The History Center, Diboll, Texas. The Carrizo-Wilcox Lufkin’s drinking water comes from this aquifer. It refills slowly, and the state measured it dropping nearly 500 feet while the paper mill pumped. The history. River and lake water the City already owns Rights to 19,100 acre-feet a year from the Angelina River, stored in Lake Kurth. That’s about 17 million gallons a day. The City can also take up to 28,000 acre-feet a year from Sam Rayburn. Reused water Treated wastewater, cleaned again for cooling. Other data centers already run on it (more below). Sources: KTRE, Feb. 2009 (19,100 acre-feet a year from the Angelina River; Kurth Lake storage); TCEQ agenda, Aug. 26, 2009 (the City may divert up to 28,000 acre-feet a year from Sam Rayburn); TWDB, Jan. 2026 approval of the regional water plans (Sam Rayburn to Kurth Lake project). 19,100 acre-feet × 325,851 gallons ÷ 365 days = about 17 million gallons a day. The City bought it for industry. In 2009 the City agreed to pay $15 million for the old paper mill’s water system: 13 wells, Lake Kurth, and the Angelina River rights. A council member said at the time that the City would be able to sell treated and untreated water to business and industry. This year, former Mayor Jack Gorden told the Lufkin Daily News: “This is the reason that water was bought for.”. For scale: City Manager Kevin Gee has said Lufkin uses about 8 million gallons a day in all. The river right alone is about twice that. And the City already plans to use more lake water. The 2026 East Texas Regional Water Plan lists a City project to pipe its Sam Rayburn water to Lake Kurth, about $136.5 million, around 2040. Sources: KTRE, Feb. 2009 ; Lufkin Daily News, “As AI data centers eye Lufkin” ; TWDB, Lake Kurth (built under a 1958 permit to Southland Paper Mills, now owned by the City). Other data centers already do this. San Antonio, Texas. Microsoft reports that 79% of the water at its San Antonio site is recycled, reused or non-potable. Microsoft, June 2026. Douglas County, Georgia. Google’s data center switched from drinking water to recycled water for cooling in 2008. Silicon UK. The state’s own water plan agrees. The East Texas Regional Water Plan says every water user in Angelina County depends on groundwater, but “both the Yegua and Carrizo-Wilcox aquifers have limited capacity for expanded development.” It says raw water from Lake Kurth is already available for industry, and it plans for new industry to buy water from the City, with Sam Rayburn as the long-term supply. Source: 2021 East Texas Regional Water Plan, Chapter 5B, Angelina County. The 2026 plan, approved by the state in January 2026, keeps the same strategy. “Why not use the salty water underground?”. We looked. Texas has mapped 31 zones of brackish (salty) groundwater set aside for heavy use. None has been added since 2019, and none is in Deep East Texas. The state is still studying the Yegua-Jackson aquifer, which runs under our part of the state. And some of the “other layers” aren’t junk water. The state found fresh water in the Yegua across Angelina County, down to a line between Huntington and Diboll, and the City of Diboll pumps from it. [Our reading] South of that line the Yegua is likely saltier, but nobody has studied it as a water supply. Salty groundwater isn’t a ready option here today. The water the City already owns is. Sources: TWDB, The Status of Brackish Aquifer Studies in Texas, Dec. 1, 2025 ; TWDB zone designations (2016: Carrizo-Wilcox south of the Colorado River, Gulf Coast, Rustler; 2019: Blossom, Nacatoch, Northern Trinity); TWDB Report 110 (1970), Yegua Formation section (fresh-water area; Diboll’s pumping). Who can make it happen. Lufkin City Council The Lufkin Daily News reported that a big industrial user would likely need a contract with the City to get water. The contract can say which water. Pineywoods Groundwater Conservation District Texas law lets a district set different rules for each aquifer, or each layer of one. It could hold the Carrizo-Wilcox to tighter limits. The Texas Legislature Lawmakers have said groundwater will be a major focus when they meet in January 2027. Sources: Lufkin Daily News ; Texas Water Code §36.116(d). What we don’t know yet. Whether the City’s Angelina River right is still in good standing, and how much river and lake water it uses today. We’ve asked for the records. Whether any water deal under discussion says which water a data center would get. What you can do. Ask the Lufkin City Council one question, out loud or by email: “Will any data center water deal require river, lake or reused water instead of the Carrizo-Wilcox, and will you put it in the contract?”.
