Side view of the water level around the well Side view, 15 miles each way from the well. The top line is where the water sits now. The red curve is where it would sit. Change the aquifer numbers How easily water moves through the sand Transmissivity, in gallons a day per foot. The state measured 14,000 to 36,000 for the Carrizo here. Lower means a deeper funnel. Distance to the outcrop How far north the sand comes up to the surface and refills. The state’s own example used 15 miles. Closer means the funnel levels off sooner. How much water the sand gives up as it drops Storage coefficient. The state used 0.00005 here. Bigger values slow how fast the funnel spreads, but not how deep it ends up. Does it match what really happened? Press Industry in 1968 and slide the time to about 30 years. A mile from the well, the model shows the water about 425 feet lower. The state measured static water levels drawn down “nearly 500 feet near the center of pumping” by 1970, after about 30 years of pumping by the mill and the cities. That’s close. The real pumping was spread over several well fields and grew over time, so it won’t match exactly. But it shows the math lands in the right neighborhood. [Our reading]. Sources: TWDB Report 110 (1970), abstract and pp. 22–23 (1968 pumping, drawdown near 500 feet); our water history. How it works. In 1970, the state’s consultants figured out how far wells would pull down the Carrizo in Angelina and Nacogdoches counties. They used a standard formula hydrologists have used since the 1930s, called the Theis equation. They treated the outcrop to the north as a line where rain refills the sand. This page runs that same math. Their own example used a well pumping 500 gallons a minute, a transmissivity of 10,000 gallons a day per foot, a storage coefficient of 0.00005, and an outcrop 15 miles away. We start with those values, except transmissivity. We use 20,000, the middle of the range the state measured for the Carrizo here. Source: TWDB Report 110 , “Coefficients of Transmissibility, Permeability, and Storage” and “Interference Between Wells and Long-Term Drawdowns,” pp. 27–34. Storage coefficients of 0.00007 to 0.0002 for the Carrizo: TWDB Report 327 (1991), p. 13. Power plant request: Powered Land , from Pineywoods GCD records. What this can’t tell you. It’s one straw in an empty glass. It shows only the new well. Every other well already pumping adds its own funnel on top. The state wrote that these funnels “are additive.”. It’s not the state’s full groundwater model. The Texas Water Development Board runs a much bigger computer model of the whole aquifer. That’s our next step. Until then, treat these numbers as a fair estimate, not a forecast. The sand isn’t the same everywhere. The state measured a wide range. Try the low and high ends under “Change the aquifer numbers.”. It doesn’t know where any project would put its wells. Amp Z hasn’t filed for a well permit, and its water use is still listed as “TBD.”. What you can do. The board that permits big wells adopted new rules for them on Nov. 9, 2026. Here’s what the rules say. Bring this page to its next meeting. Ask them how far the water would drop if a big new user moved in, and whether they’ve run the numbers. Here’s how to speak up

sections.t: Seven big projects in Angelina County
sections.x: East Texas Legacy Coalition. Seven big projects are lined up for Angelina County. Two data centers, two gas power plants, a solar farm and two battery sites. Here is what each one is, how big it is, and what we know about its water. Every fact has its source underneath. How big, side by side. Each block below is drawn to scale by its size in megawatts. HyperDataGrid isn’t on it because no size for it is on public record yet. Amp Z. Amp Z data center, 2,100 MW. Longleaf gas plant, 600 MW. Longleaf II gas plant, 600 MW. Sun Angel batteries, 202 MW. Azalea Springs Solar, 181 MW. North Herty batteries, 126 MW. Amp Z alone is bigger than the other five on this line put together. One thing to know: the data center’s number is how much power it plans to use. The other five are how much power they would make or store. A megawatt is a megawatt either way, which is why we put them on one line. What “in the grid queue” means. ERCOT runs the Texas power grid. Any project that wants to plug in has to get in line first, and ERCOT publishes that line every month. Being in line doesn’t mean a project will get built. It means a company has paid to study plugging in here, and it’s the earliest public sign that something is coming. Source: ERCOT Generation Interconnection Status report , data as of Oct. 22, 2026. Each project, in plain words. Amp Z data center. AI data center, 2,100 MW planned. Where. The old Southland paper mill on Highway 103 East near Herty, just outside Lufkin. About 1,041 acres under option. Power. The landowner, Verdant Industries, holds a January 2025 state air permit for 12 natural gas turbines on the site. Water. The public was told about 500 gallons a day. The company’s county tax application lists its water needs as “TBD.” It has filed no well permits with the groundwater district, and the City of Lufkin owns the old mill’s wells. What happened to our water the last time this site pumped. Water, in the City’s own emails. July 28, 2025: a developer representative asked whether the City could deliver 20 million gallons a day to the mill site. Aug. 8, 2025: the same representative asked the City to confirm it could likely supply about 17 million gallons a day of raw water from Kurth Lake. Sept. 16, 2025: Amp Z asked for a “will serve” letter stating 20 million gallons a day of municipal water plus another 17 million of surface water , adding that it didn’t expect to use that much. Sept. 17, 2025: the city manager wrote to the economic development director, “We do not want to say we have 20 [million] gallons and 17 [million] available for their project.” Sept. 25, 2025: the City’s letter cited about 17 million gallons a day of surface water capacity, plus high-capacity wells, and committed no volume. Feb. 5, 2026: the City’s press release said 20 million gallons a day was the old mill system’s “total system capacity” and that the project expected about 15,000 gallons a month, “similar to the water usage of three homes.”. Taxes. Angelina County turned down its request for a 10-year tax break. Who decides: the City. The site is in Lufkin’s Industrial District No. 1. In the City’s 2022 agreement with the landowner, Verdant, the City guaranteed the site stays outside city limits and immune from annexation through 2032 (with a narrow exception for land owned by others), and agreed to provide the landowner water and sewer “at in City rates” for that term. The agreement can’t be assigned: if the land is sold, the buyer gets those terms only by entering its own Industrial District Agreement with the City. On Feb. 5, 2026, City and Amp Z emails carried the subject line “IDA & De-annexation catch up - (Amp Z & City of Lufkin),” and the City shared its press release with Amp Z before issuing it. Who decides: the County. Angelina County Commissioners Court votes on any tax break and any road-use agreement. In June, County Judge Keith Wright pledged that no tax-break proposal would come before the court unless the developer first holds a public meeting for county residents. In August the court hired outside counsel for data center tax-abatement agreements, and in October it paid for legal help drafting a road-use agreement with AMP Z Champion Data Center Holdings LLC (Twin Oaks and John Kolb roads). Sources: Lufkin Daily News (acreage); Lufkin Daily News (turbines); City of Lufkin Data Center FAQ (500 gallons); Angelina County records produced to ETLC (tax application); Pineywoods GCD email to ETLC, Sept. 22, 2026 (no well permits); Lufkin Daily News (tax break rejected); Powered Land ; City of Lufkin emails released to ETLC under request CRR-2026-315 (Item 11, water availability, July–Sept. 2025; Item 8, Feb. 5, 2026); City letter to Amp Z, Sept. 25, 2025 ; 2022 Verdant Industrial District Agreement , Sections IV, XIV and XVI; The 936 (July 2026 print edition, county pledge; Sept. 2026 print edition, outside counsel; Oct. 25, 2026, road-use agreement). HyperDataGrid data center. Data center, size not on record. Where. The old Northern Chip Mill on Ben Dunn Road, off Highway 103 West. Water. The developer told the groundwater district it would use about 500 gallons a day, then asked for 13 million gallons a year from the wells on the property. That’s just under the 15 million that would require a public hearing. As of Sept. 29, 2026, the district had taken no action. Who decides. The Pineywoods district. Under 15 million gallons a year, the request doesn’t need a board meeting or public hearing, the district’s general manager wrote to the developer. Source: Pineywoods GCD emails to ETLC, Aug.–Sept. 2026; Powered Land. Longleaf Power Station. Natural gas power plant, 600 MW. Who. Long Leaf Generating LLC, part of WattBridge. Where. North of Lufkin near Kurth Lake, connecting at the Redland substation. Water. Approved for 80 million gallons a year and never drilled. In March 2026 it switched to running around the clock and asked for 1.5 billion gallons a year , about 4.1 million gallons a day. That request has been on hold since July 2026 at the company’s request. Taxes. The County approved a 10-year tax break in May 2025, on the condition that it run as a “peaking” plant, only when demand is high. A plant that runs around the clock isn’t a peaking plant. That change may break the terms of its tax break. [Our reading of the records; the County hasn’t said.] Sources: ERCOT queue, project 26INR0294; Pineywoods GCD email to ETLC, Sept. 22, 2026; Lufkin Daily News (tax break). Longleaf II Power Station. Natural gas power plant, 600 MW. Who. WattBridge Texas Holdings, the same company behind Longleaf. When. Projected to come online July 2030. Water. We have no water records for this one yet. This is a separate request from the first Longleaf, with its own ERCOT number. Together the two would be 1,200 MW of gas power from one company. Source: ERCOT queue, project 30INR0114. Sun Angel ESS. Battery storage, 202 MW. What. A battery site that soaks up power from the grid and sends it back later. “ESS” stands for energy storage system. When. Projected to come online September 2028. Where. ERCOT lists it only as Angelina County. Source: ERCOT queue, project 27INR0247. Azalea Springs Solar. Solar farm, 181 MW. When. Projected to come online Nov. 1, 2026 , the soonest of these projects. That date has passed. We’re checking ERCOT’s newest report to see where it stands. Where. ERCOT lists it only as Angelina County. Source: ERCOT queue, project 19INR0110. ERCOT’s projected dates often slip. Solar Star North Herty Storage. Battery storage, 126 MW. When. Projected to come online August 2027. Where. The name points to the Herty area. ERCOT lists it only as Angelina County. Source: ERCOT queue, project 24INR0174. What you can do with this. Share this page with one person who doesn’t know any of this is coming. Watch the Lufkin City Council and Pineywoods board agendas. Both have to post at least 72 hours before they meet. Here’s how to speak up. Look up your own county: Angelina County Watch updates these numbers every night and helps you write a records request in a few minutes

East Texas Legacy Coalition. This is your home. You get a say. They’ll tell you it’s outside city limits, the county can’t zone it, and it’s already decided. That’s not the whole story. Four public bodies have a hand in what happens here, and every one of them answers to you. It’s already working. Don’t let anybody tell you showing up doesn’t matter. Here’s what happened after folks did. June 2026 Residents pack the Commissioners Court and won’t sit quiet about water, power, noise and wastewater. July 14, 2026 Commissioners vote unanimously for Resolution 010-26, asking Austin to let counties require water impact statements, public hearings, noise limits and setbacks for big data centers. August 2026 The City of Lufkin passes a similar resolution backing the county. October 2026 The county has turned down Amp Z’s request for a 10-year tax break. Sources: Lufkin Daily News (June meeting, Resolution 010-26); Lufkin Daily News (what the resolution asks for; tax break rejected); Lufkin Daily News (City resolution in August). Coming up. Mark your calendar. Mon., Dec. 1 · Lufkin City Council Lufkin City Council meets The council’s proposed cap on public records requests may come back up. The agenda posts the week before; check it at cityoflufkin.com. Date not set yet Pineywoods hearing on the Pitman Farms well permits The district says timely requests to contest the permits will go to a preliminary hearing to decide who gets party status. It will post notice at pgcd.org. What we know. Tues., Jan. 12, 2027 The Texas Legislature goes back to work That’s when Resolution 010-26 either becomes a bill or gathers dust. Sources: Pineywoods General Manager Wil Blough, emails to ETLC, Nov. 19 and 20, 2026 (Pitman hearing); Pineywoods GCD ; KTRE (Jan. 12, 2027). The rules Pineywoods voted on Nov. 9. Update: the board passed its rules on Nov. 9. See what passed and the loophole that stayed open. Here’s what was proposed going in. Pineywoods is proposing rules that do a lot of what we’ve been asking for. Big pumpers get watched. Projects permitted for more than 1,500 acre-feet a year, about 1.3 million gallons a day, must drill monitoring wells at their property line before they pump. If the water drops 50 feet below where it started for three months in a row, the District suspends or cuts the permit until it comes back. Companies can’t split one big project into smaller permits to get around it. Every data center and power plant gets a monitoring well. Any size. The company pays, and the water levels report straight to the District by cell and satellite. No more secret water deals. Anyone applying for a permit has to prove they own the right to that water and show any deal that transferred it. Those deals have to be filed in the county deed records, where anyone can look them up. The gap. The 50-foot shutoff doesn’t apply to a city water utility serving its own area. If a data center buys City water instead of drilling its own wells, the shutoff may never kick in. [Our reading]. What to ask: Thank the board for the good parts. Then ask them to close the gap, so a big user is watched no matter whose wells the water comes from. Source: Pineywoods GCD proposed rule amendments , draft dated Oct. 6, 2026 (Rules 5.15 and 5.16) and proposed Rule 5.4(m). These are proposals until the board votes. Four doors. Here’s how to knock. Lufkin City Council. What it controls. City water. A big industrial user would likely need a contract with the City to get it. When. Usually the 1st and 3rd Tuesday of the month, 5 p.m., City Hall, 300 E. Shepherd Ave. How. Email your council member and the mayor. Ask them to put data center water on the agenda. The catch: At Council you can only speak on items that are on that night’s agenda. In May, residents who came to talk about data centers were sent back to their seats. So the ask is simple: put it on the agenda. Sources: Lufkin City Charter (meeting schedule); Lufkin Daily News (water contract); KTRE, May 2026 (agenda-only comment). Angelina County Commissioners Court. What it controls. Tax breaks and road use agreements. Right now those are the county’s only real leverage over a data center. When. Tuesday mornings at 10, usually twice a month, 211 E. Shepherd Ave. County calendar. How. Every regular agenda has a Public Forum. Sign in, stand up, say your piece. Sources: KTRE (county leverage); County agenda, Sept. 8, 2026 (time, place, Public Forum). Pineywoods Groundwater Conservation District. What it controls. Permits for big water wells in Angelina and Nacogdoches counties. When. Next meeting: check the posted agenda at pgcd.org. How. Show up for the public hearing, or email the District at staff@pgcd.org before the meeting so your comment is on file. Who sits on it. Seven directors appointed by the City of Lufkin, the City of Nacogdoches, and the two counties. Three seats expire Dec. 31, 2026: Gloria Montes and Greg Grigsby (appointed by Nacogdoches County) and Roger Russell (appointed by Angelina and Nacogdoches counties). Your opening: The commissioners courts pick who fills those seats. Go to Public Forum and ask who they plan to appoint, and whether that person will protect the aquifer. Sources: Pineywoods GCD ; Pineywoods board page and its 2026 director terms list. The Texas Legislature. What it controls. Whether counties get any power over data centers at all. When. Session starts Jan. 12, 2027. How. Look up your state representative and senator. Call or write and ask them to carry Resolution 010-26 into law. Source: KTRE. What to say. You don’t need a speech. Your name, where you live, and one sentence: “This is my home. Leave the Carrizo-Wilcox for the people who drink it, and put it in writing before anybody signs a deal.”. At the next Pineywoods meeting, try: “Thank you for watching the big pumpers. Please make sure a data center is watched even when it buys City water.”. Say it in your own words. A grandmother talking about her well beats a lawyer every time. Want to do more? Ask for the records yourself. Our Angelina County Watch page will help you write a public records request in a few minutes. Bring one neighbor. Ten people in a room changes the room. Join the coalition. We’ll post every meeting that matters , so you don’t have to hunt for them

sections.t: They Heard You. Then They Passed It Anyway.
sections.x: East Texas Legacy Coalition. Tuesday, November 10, 2026. Updated Friday, November 20, 2026, with the district's answer on the Pitman hearing; earlier update Nov. 11 with Lufkin Daily News reporting and a recording of the meeting. They Heard You. Then They Passed It Anyway. What the Pineywoods Groundwater District passed on November 9, and why it matters. By Fawn Elizabeth Zion, founder, East Texas Legacy Coalition. On Monday, November 9, the Pineywoods Groundwater Conservation District board unanimously passed its new rules exactly as written, after hours of public opposition. Those rules weaken pumping cutbacks for deep wells. They also keep an exemption that lets a city resell water to a data center without the new data center monitoring. The East Texas Legacy Coalition asked the board, in writing and on the record, to close that exemption. They didn't. What happened Monday. The board met at 1:30 p.m. at Kurth Lake Lodge. It held a public hearing on proposed rule changes and on five high-capacity well permits requested by Pitman Farms, followed by a business meeting. Residents, landowners and water utility officials spoke for hours, most of them opposed. On November 3, the district's general manager wrote that his office was “inundated with unanticipated public comments.”. The board didn't act on the Pitman permits. Neighboring property owners have contested them, and a preliminary hearing will be held at a later date. It did act on the rules. I called general manager Wil Blough at 8:56 a.m. on November 10. He told me the board passed the rule amendments as proposed, then confirmed it in writing that morning: the board adopted the amendments as written, and the vote was unanimous except for board president Kevin Gee, who wasn't at the meeting. The Daily Sentinel reports the vote came near the end of a meeting that ran about three hours. The Daily Sentinel reports that about 150 people came to oppose the permits. Once they heard there'd be no action on the permits, most of them left before the board discussed and voted on the rules. The vote came about an hour after most of that standing-room-only crowd had gone. People who attended told us they left believing there'd be no vote that day. The rule change. Rule 5.15 lets the district cut back or suspend big pumping when water levels drop. A 50-foot drop for three straight months can trigger it. A 75-foot drop brings more restrictions. The new rule exempts deep Wilcox wells, below 1,500 feet, pumping under 4,000 acre-feet a year. Those wells still get monitored, but the cutbacks no longer apply. Pitman Farms has asked for 3,363 acre-feet a year from wells 1,900 to 2,300 feet deep. That fits right under the line. The Daily Sentinel describes these as the rule changes requested by Pitman Farms. The district's own hydrogeologist said the exemption is meant partly to steer industry toward deeper, more mineralized water instead of competing with public water systems. The loophole that stayed open. The new rules require real-time monitoring wells for data centers. That's a real protection. But the rule says it “does not apply to a retail public water utility if the water is used to provide for its service needs within its service area within the District.” Another rule, 7.1(b)(4), has a similar exemption. In plain English: a city can pump groundwater and sell it to a data center inside its service area, and the data center monitoring never kicks in. We asked the board to close that for new industrial sales over 100,000 gallons a day. They passed the rules without that change. Why it matters in Lufkin. 2009 In a contract between the City of Lufkin and the mill's then-owner, Abitibi-Consolidated, a water addendum requires the city to supply up to 5 million gallons a day to the seller “or its assignee” for 20 years, with two 10-year renewals. Sept. 25, 2025 In a letter to Amp Z, signed by City Manager Kevin Gee, the city calls the data center site “within our service area” and says it owns “several high-capacity water wells in proximity that could be utilized in serving this location.”. March 6, 2026 The 936 reports Amp Z's proposed 2.1-gigawatt AI data center, Project Lufkin, at the old Southland mill site. March 23, 2026 District minutes record board president Kevin Gee saying the data center at the old paper mill would use City of Lufkin water. Nov. 2, 2026 The city says it can't find Exhibit D-1, the district well permits that were supposed to be attached to the 2009 water deal. Whether that 5 million gallon reservation has been handed off to anyone is still an open records request. Nov. 2026 The Lufkin City Council accepts Gee's resignation as city manager. The district's own website lists Kevin Gee as board president, appointed by the City of Lufkin. The general manager confirmed in writing that Gee wasn't at Monday's meeting. Board treasurer Tommy Carswell is general manager of Four Way Special Utility District, a water utility in the district. The same exemption covers it. Not the first time. District records we obtained through the Public Information Act show a buyer looking at land at 3641 Ben Dunn Road, on Highway 103 West, for a data center. He asked the general manager in writing how to avoid a public hearing. The general manager answered in writing, laying out the limits that trigger one. The Pitman Farms application. Pitman Farms wants five wells for a poultry processing plant on FM 225, about nine miles west of Nacogdoches, near Lake Nacogdoches. That's 3,363 acre-feet a year, about 3 million gallons a day, or nearly 1.1 billion gallons a year. The company's own hydrogeologist admitted its modeling predicts drops beyond the district's existing limits. He said those are pressure changes, not draining the aquifer, and that clay layers separate the deep Wilcox from the shallower Carrizo. He couldn't say whether the study used the updated groundwater model released in January 2026. No one presented evidence at the meeting that these wells are meant for a data center. Who voted. Every director at the meeting voted yes. Board president Kevin Gee was absent. Among those voting yes was Director Gloria Montes, who is also president of D&M Water Supply Corporation, according to D&M's own website. At the same hearing, D&M's general manager, Charles Perkins, told the board his utility strongly opposes the Pitman permits. We've asked the district for any written comments D&M submitted, and we'll publish what we get. What people said. Mary Reed, whose family has a well about two miles from the site, said the 4,000 acre-foot line “fits one application almost exactly.” She said the company's own report predicts pressure drops of 300 to 400 feet near the wells. Charles Perkins, general manager of D&M Water Supply, said his utility strongly opposes the permits. He said 3 million gallons a day is nearly twice D&M's entire daily capacity and about 37.5% of what Nacogdoches pumps each day. Others raised wastewater, truck traffic, odor, property values, and Lake Nacogdoches. Several said monitoring means little if the district gives up its power to order cutbacks. Thank you to every neighbor, landowner and group who showed up, including Bobby Tillman, who just ran for state senate, and our partners at Protect Our Piney Woods. The same night. According to a recording of the meeting shared with us by a coalition partner who attended: The board voted to recommend that Groundwater Management Area 11 go back to an older standard, Scenario 33, instead of the Scenario 26.1 proposal now on the table. In the same discussion, the board described the difference for Angelina and Nacogdoches counties as minimal. GMA 11's own draft report found that under Scenario 33, nine counties would exceed a 10% share of dry wells by 2080, while Scenario 26.1 keeps every county under that line, the Lufkin Daily News reported. The board voted to ask state legislators to raise the cap on its production fee from 2.5 cents to as much as 10 cents per 1,000 gallons, saying its budget is running short. A district report said a 1.5-billion-gallon water request tied to a planned power plant is on indefinite hold. The transcript is auto-generated, so we paraphrase rather than quote. We've requested the official recording. Nov. 18 result: GMA 11 voted 3 to 1 to keep using Scenario 33 through 2080, instead of switching to the proposed alternative meant to curb projected groundwater declines and scale back future pumping limits. Panola County GCD's Mike Pennington cast the only vote against. Dozens of residents came to speak. Sources: Nicole Bradford, The Daily Sentinel, Nov. 19, 2026 ; KETK, Nov. 18, 2026. Background on the vote →. Since Monday. The Lufkin Daily News reported on Nov. 11 that after announcing there would be no vote on the Pitman permits, the board moved the rule changes from near the top of the agenda to the very end, then approved them about an hour after most of the crowd had left. Nacogdoches County's Republican chair, Brian Fitzgerald, and Democratic chair, John Watt, are now working together against the change. They plan to ask the Nacogdoches County Commissioners Court for an agenda item so residents can raise it there. What we did. The East Texas Legacy Coalition couldn't be there in person, so we did the homework. We sent written comments on October 31, before the deadline, and more on November 5 when new city records came in. The general manager confirmed in writing that both went into the public record and to the board. To be fair. The agenda, posted October 16, said “action may be taken” and listed “Discuss and possibly approve rule amendments.” So they were allowed to vote Monday. The same agenda also listed possibly pursuing a change to the state law that created the district. We don't know yet whether they acted on that. What we still don't know. Exactly which directors were there, including who sat in the seat Greg Grigsby held. Whether they acted on changing the district's founding law. When the adopted rules will be posted; the general manager says the district is still updating that document. We requested the minutes, the full recording, the vote record and the adopted rule text on Nov. 10, and the scenario modeling on Nov. 11. What you can do. If you own land in Angelina or Nacogdoches County, you can petition the district to change its rules. Texas Water Code 36.1025 gives landowners that right. The district has 90 days to either start the rule change or put in writing why it won't. We'll help draft it. One petition is easy to ignore. Fifty aren't. If you live or own land near FM 225, call the district at 936-568-9292 and ask how to take part in the Pitman Farms permit hearing. Talk to the people who appoint this board: the Angelina and Nacogdoches County commissioners courts, and the Lufkin and Nacogdoches city councils. Kevin Gee's seat belongs to the Lufkin City Council. Show up at public comment and ask who they're putting on that board, and why. A preliminary hearing on the contested Pitman permits is expected later in November, the Lufkin Daily News reports. No date has been posted yet. The regional groundwater planning group, GMA-11, meets November 18. The district board's next meeting is 1:30 p.m. Monday, February 8, at Kurth Lake Lodge, 1420 Kurth Lake Road, Lufkin. Update, Nov. 20: the Pitman Farms hearing. Pineywoods General Manager Wil Blough told ETLC in writing on Nov. 20 that timely requests to contest the Pitman Farms permit applications will go to a preliminary hearing to decide who gets party status, and that the date for that hearing hasn't been set. He also wrote that all notices for permit hearings will comply with the district's rules and state law. On Nov. 19 he added ETLC to the district's list for written notice of hearings, and said the district will post notice on its website, pgcd.org. Want notice too? Anyone can ask in writing under District Rule 16.2(d). Email gm@pgcd.org and ask to be notified of any hearing on the Pitman Farms applications. sections.t: Mill Creek: sewage, a fish kill and 200,000 gallons of drinking water
sections.x: East Texas Legacy Coalition. Sewage, a fish kill, and 200,000 gallons of drinking water. In August 2023, sewage spills from a Lufkin lift station caused a fish kill in Mill Creek. Here’s what the state’s own order says happened, and what the City paid. What happened. When. Aug. 26 to 29, 2023. Where. The Ellen Trout lift station, part of the City’s Hurricane Creek wastewater system. What. Clogged and inoperable pumps, plus pump servicing, let about 6,100 gallons of untreated sewage out in two spills. Fish died. A landowner whose property Mill Creek runs through reported the fish kill on Aug. 28. Cleanup. The City fixed the pumps by Aug. 31 and flushed the creek and a nearby stream with about 200,000 gallons of drinking water from a public water tank. Source: TCEQ Agreed Order 2024-0641-MWD-E , Findings of Fact 2 and 3, and the Executive Summary. What the City paid. Penalty. $75,000. To the state. $0 to the state’s general fund. The whole $75,000 is offset if the City finishes a project: an alarm and monitoring system (SCADA) for its lift stations, with an estimated cost of $1,873,023. If the City doesn’t finish it, the state can demand the money. Signed. By Mayor Mark Hicks on June 15, 2026, and for TCEQ’s executive director on July 25, 2026. Source: the same order, Conclusion of Law 4, the signature page and Attachment A. It wasn’t a one-time thing. The compliance history filed with this order shows the Hurricane Creek plant reported its own failure to meet one or more permit limits every month from July 2023 through September 2024 , 15 months in a row. TCEQ still rated the City “Satisfactory.”. An earlier order, 2020-1536-MWD-E, took effect Feb. 27, 2024, also for sewage discharges. And a separate case, 2024-0119-MWD-E, lists 14 violations at the same plant, with a proposed penalty of $193,813, again with $0 to the state’s general fund. That one was on TCEQ’s Oct. 21, 2026 agenda, and we haven’t confirmed the final outcome. Sources: TCEQ Compliance History Report in the order above (Section A and Appendix A); KLTV, Oct. 23, 2026, and The 936, Oct. 24, 2026, on case 2024-0119-MWD-E. Why it matters now. A data center is planned for the old paper mill site, and the site’s owner is renewing the mill’s old wastewater permit, which allows discharges averaging up to 5 million gallons a day into Paper Mill Creek, the Angelina River and Sam Rayburn Reservoir. [Our reading: before anybody approves more wastewater here, the public deserves to know who will treat it and how.]. Source on the permit renewal: Powered Land. See also the seven projects and our water history. What you can do. Read the full order yourself. It’s 24 pages and public. Ask the City Council whether the alarm system is finished. sections.t: Selling it before they own it: 1606 Corp. and the old Lufkin power plant
sections.x: East Texas Legacy Coalition. Selling it before they own it. A Nevada company called 1606 Corp. has been trying to buy the old biomass power plant in North Lufkin since spring. Its deadline to close was Oct. 31. As of Nov. 20, we haven’t found a filing or news story saying whether it closed. By its own account, it still didn’t have the money, and it was already shopping the site to AI data centers and to a possible buyer for its contract. The deal. What. About 132 acres and a 55-megawatt biomass power plant in North Lufkin. Buyer. 1606 Corp., a penny-stock company that trades over the counter as CBDW. Plan. Use the plant’s power to run AI data centers right on site. Deadline. Oct. 31, 2026. It was supposed to close April 15, then May 22. It’s been pushed back several times. As of Nov. 20, we haven’t found word on whether it closed. Sources: 1606 Corp. SEC filing, Sept. 8, 2026 ; Lufkin Daily News (April and May dates); Lufkin Daily News (the purchase agreement). In their own words. You don’t have to take our word for any of this. It’s all in what 1606 has told the federal government and its own investors: They don’t have the money. Closing depends on financing that, by their own account, hasn’t been secured. It may never close. They say there’s no guarantee the purchase happens by Oct. 31, or at all. They’re already shopping it. They hired MDM Group to take the site to hyperscale operators, AI companies and investors. They might flip it. One option they list is selling or handing off their contract to buy the plant to somebody else. On Sept. 6 they signed a non-binding letter of intent with Prime Tex Group, which they describe as an industrial group with timber and sawmill operations, to look at doing exactly that. The plant may not even run. It’s being bought “as-is,” and the seller makes no promise the equipment works. The title isn’t clean. Pending tax and other lawsuits affect the property, and 1606 says it can’t promise those get resolved. They’ve got money on the line. They’ve paid non-refundable fees they lose if the deal falls apart. Sources: 1606 Corp. press release, Aug. 25, 2026 (MDM Group, financing, possible sale or assignment of the contract); 1606 Corp. press release, Sept. 16, 2026 (Prime Tex letter of intent); 1606 Corp. SEC filing, Sept. 8, 2026 (as-is condition, pending litigation, non-refundable fees, Oct. 31 deadline). Here’s what this looks like to us [Our reading]. A company that can’t pay for a power plant is out pitching it to data centers before the ink’s dry. That looks like a company hoping somebody with deep pockets shows up to pay for a purchase it can’t finance on its own, or takes the contract off its hands. Either way, the folks deciding what happens to that site are investors and data center companies. Nobody’s asked the people who live here. What we don’t know yet. Whether the deal closed by Oct. 31, got pushed back again, or fell apart. Which data center companies MDM has pitched, and whether any of them bit. Where a data center on this site would get its water. What happens next. 1606 has to tell its investors what happened with the deal. We’re watching for its next SEC filing and will update this page when it lands. Know somebody who should see this? Join the coalition , and share this page

sections.h: Every ring was laid down by somebody who thought this place was worth keeping
sections.x: Count the rings. Every ring was laid down by somebody who thought this place was worth keeping. A thousand years in the Piney Woods, one ring at a time. Swipe through, then dig into the whole story. c. 800 Caddo country. Caddo people built a village and ceremonial center on a bluff above the Neches. Three earthen mounds still rise out of the pines near Alto. Read the ring →. 1690 The King’s Road comes through. The first mission in the province of Texas went up in a Caddo village near present-day Weches. A stretch of El Camino Real still runs through the pines. Read the ring →. 1882–1903 Rails, sawdust and new towns. The railroad made Lufkin in 1882. Then the timber boom: sawmills, company stores and log trains running into Diboll. Read the ring →. 1936 Cutover land gets a second chance. Stumps and worn-out farms became the Angelina, Davy Crockett, Sabine and Sam Houston national forests. The pines you drive through grew back. Read the ring →. 1974 East Texans saved the Big Thicket. Not because Washington noticed. Because local people wouldn’t quit until it became one of the country’s first national preserves. Read the ring →. Today The next ring is ours. The water under our feet is the next fight, and it’s the same kind of fight. Read the ring →. Swipe or scroll sideways for more →. sections.h: The towns, the rivers and the people in between
sections.x: Places and families. The towns, the rivers and the people in between. Some of these places are still on the map. Some are under a lake. All of them belong to somebody’s family. Huntington. A railroad town laid out and auctioned off in the summer of 1900, with a library built to honor its WWII dead. Lost to the lake. Concord, family farms and graves moved when Sam Rayburn filled. Our water has a paper trail. From a water-powered mill on Mill Creek to a reservoir built for industry. Who decides the route? Railroads, a paper mill and a million acres owned from New York. 1848–1942. The founder’s great-great-great-grandfather. W. D. “Bill” Russell. Came to Texas as a boy of five. When he died in 1942 he was Angelina County’s last surviving Confederate veteran. He’s buried at Jonesville Cemetery near Huntington. 1957. The founder’s grandfather. Hayden Russell. Played on the Lufkin PONY League All-Stars that won the 1957 PONY League World Series, 5–2 over Maywood, Illinois. Read the family’s story → · Got a photo of your people? sections.h: The ones who stood up for this place

A man with no formal schooling who knew just about every plant in the Big Thicket. And the neighbors who wouldn’t quit. Lady Bird Johnson. Lance Rosier, “Mr. Big Thicket”. He hunted flowers, not game. By the 1960s, anyone who wanted to understand the Thicket came to him, and in 1965 he guided Senator Yarborough through it.
